title: READ ME FIRST -- bis_knowledge_v2.jsonl schema, changes and known limitations
content:
This is a revised build (schema_version 2.0) of the original bis_knowledge.jsonl BIS procurement knowledge base. Total records: 4385 (original 4378 records, retained and enriched in place, plus 7 new web-researched mandatory_certifications records). 

CHANGES FROM V1 (all mechanical/structural, or clearly source-attributed additions -- nothing was fabricated):
1. Fixed character-encoding artifacts (mojibake, stray '?' substitutions) in 6 records (6 flagged with data_quality_flags=['encoding_artifact_fixed']).
2. Added `status_parsed`: the free-text `status` field (70+ ad-hoc variants in v1) is now also expressed as structured booleans (is_current, is_mandatory, is_superseded, is_withdrawn, is_suspended), a normalized `revision` label, and an extracted `status_date` where present. Original `status` string is preserved unchanged.
3. Added `date_precision` (day/month/year/unknown) alongside the untouched original `date`.
4. Added `related_standards_resolved`: each entry in `related_standards` is matched against every `standard_number` in the KB using a normalized IS-family key (handles missing part/year suffixes). Resolution rate rose from ~23% (exact string match) to ~97% (family-level match).
5. Added `standard_family_key` and `same_family_ids` on every record: records sharing the same base IS number (e.g. a standard_catalog_entry and a product_manual for the same standard) are now explicitly cross-linked regardless of their original id-prefix silo (isc-/pman-/qco-/etc.), so retrieval can surface related material together.
6. Added `content_depth` ('detailed' | 'descriptive' | 'directory_listing' | 'catalog_stub') and, for catalog_stub records, a `coverage_note` making explicit that the record contains only a title/IS-number/scope-keyword and NOT the standard's actual technical requirements -- so a RAG answer can flag low-evidence citations instead of overstating confidence.
7. Added 7 new, individually web-researched mandatory_certifications records (id prefix mc2-) covering QCOs absent from the original 26-record set: two-wheeler helmets (IS 4151:2015), domestic pressure cookers (IS 2347), three footwear QCOs (leather; rubber/polymeric; PPE footwear), a 2026 cookware/utensils QCO, and the 2026 Transition Facilitation Order. Each carries `source_name`='Research-compiled (web-verified, non-BIS-site sources)' (NOT scraped from bis.gov.in like the rest of the KB), a `research_basis` list of the URLs consulted, and a `gazette_verified` flag that is False wherever the exact gazette S.O./G.S.R. number could not be independently confirmed (left null rather than invented).

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE (still open gaps -- do not assume these are fixed):
- Full clause-level technical content (dimensions, tolerances, chemical-composition limits, test methods) for the ~1297 standard_catalog_entry stub records. BIS sells the full text of Indian Standards; it is not freely reproducible at scale, and inventing specific technical/safety parameters would be actively dangerous for a compliance tool. Only the 20 original 'detailed' records (clause-level content for IS 2062 and IS 1786) have this depth. Closing this gap requires licensed/authorized ingestion of the actual IS standard texts.
- A comprehensive rebuild of all ~187 real QCOs / ~769 covered product categories (the mandatory_certifications domain now has 33 records / ~25 distinct orders -- an improvement on the original 26/18, but still a small fraction of real mandatory certification coverage). Priority product categories still missing a dedicated record include furniture, air conditioners, hinges, washing machines, household water heaters (their existence is confirmed via mc2-007's Transition Facilitation Order reference, but no individual order record was added), packaged drinking water, LED lighting, and most food/chemical QCOs beyond the handful already present.
- Hallmarking-centre contact listings remain unverified against live BIS registry data as of this build; some Recognition Number validities in the original file may have since lapsed or been renewed.
- Language coverage remains English-only.

RECOMMENDED USE: filter/boost on `content_depth` and `status_parsed.is_current` at retrieval time, always surface `coverage_note` (when present) alongside any answer built from a catalog_stub record, and treat `gazette_verified=False` records as needing confirmation before being cited in an official compliance determination.

title: Origin of BIS: from the Indian Standards Institution (ISI) to the Bureau of Indian Standards
content: The Bureau of Indian Standards traces its origin to the Indian Standards Institution (ISI), which was established on 6 January 1947 as a registered society to promote standardization and quality control for India's early industrialization. ISI functioned until it was replaced by the Bureau of Indian Standards, set up under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986, which came into force on 1 April 1987. BIS marks 6 January as its Foundation Day, tracing continuity back to ISI's founding.

title: Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 - legal basis of BIS
content: The Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 was notified on 22 March 2016 and came into force on 12 October 2017, superseding the earlier BIS Act, 1986. The 2016 Act establishes BIS as India's National Standards Body for the harmonious development of standardization, conformity assessment, and quality assurance of goods, articles, processes, systems, and services. BIS functions under the administrative control of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, Government of India.

title: Core functions of BIS
content: BIS carries out five core activities: developing and publishing Indian Standards; implementing conformity assessment (certification) schemes; recognizing and operating laboratories for conformity assessment testing; implementing the Hallmarking scheme for gold and silver jewellery; and consumer empowerment and capacity-building activities. BIS also represents India in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC).

title: Formulation of Indian Standards through Division Councils and Technical Committees
content: Formulation of Indian Standards is one of BIS's core activities, carried out through 16 Division Councils that represent diverse sectors of the economy and technology, including areas such as Chemicals, Mechanical Engineering, Management and Systems, and Ayush. Under these Division Councils, technical committees comprising government, industry, and consumer representatives draft and revise Indian Standards.

title: Standards development: Wide Circulation Drafts and proposals for new standards
content: BIS publishes proposals for new Indian Standards and issues Wide Circulation Drafts (WCDs) for public and stakeholder comment before a standard is finalized. BIS also maintains lists of standards under review for revision or reaffirmation. These processes are managed through the standards.bis.gov.in portal, which lists technical departments, published standards by department, and drafts open for comment.

title: IS 456:2000 - Plain and Reinforced Concrete, Code of Practice
content: IS 456:2000 'Plain and Reinforced Concrete - Code of Practice' (fourth revision) is BIS's foundational code for the general structural use of plain and reinforced concrete in India. It provides requirements for materials, workmanship, inspection, testing, general design considerations, and structural design using both the limit state method and the working stress method (the limit state method is the recommended approach). The standard is administered by BIS's Civil Engineering Division and was reaffirmed after 2000 with subsequent amendments.

title: IS 456:2000 - structure of the code (sections and annexes)
content: IS 456:2000 is organized into sections covering: Section 1 General (scope, terminology, symbols); Section 2 Materials, Workmanship, Inspection and Testing; Section 3 General Design Considerations; Section 4 Special Design Requirements for Structural Members and Systems; and Section 5 Structural Design using the Limit State Method, supplemented by several annexes including Annex B, which retains the working stress method for legacy design practice.

title: IS 456:2000 - related and referenced standards
content: IS 456:2000 is used together with several supplementary Indian Standards: IS 383:2016 for coarse and fine aggregates for concrete; IS 516 (Part 1/Sec 1):2021 and IS 516:1959 for methods of testing hardened concrete strength; IS 1343 for prestressed concrete; IS 13920:2016 for ductile detailing of reinforced concrete structures subjected to seismic forces; and IS 1786:2008 for the deformed steel bars used as reinforcement.

title: IS 269:2015 - Ordinary Portland Cement specification (sixth revision)
content: IS 269:2015 'Ordinary Portland Cement - Specification' (sixth revision) is the Indian Standard governing ordinary Portland cement, one of the core material standards referenced alongside IS 456:2000 in construction. BIS's civil engineering standards catalogue lists it with other cement standards such as IS 455:2015 (Portland slag cement, fifth revision) and IS 383:2016 (aggregates for concrete, third revision).

title: IS 2062:2011 - Hot Rolled Medium and High Tensile Structural Steel, Specification
content: IS 2062:2011 'Hot Rolled Medium and High Tensile Structural Steel - Specification' covers requirements for steel including micro-alloyed steel plates, strips, shapes, sections (angles, tees, beams, channels), flats and bars used in structural work. The steels covered are suitable for welded, bolted and riveted structures and for general engineering purposes; where welding is used and guaranteed weldability is required, the welding procedure is to follow IS 9595:1996.

title: IS 2062:2011 - steel grade designations
content: IS 2062:2011 defines structural steel grade designations using the 'E' system reflecting minimum yield strength, including grades such as E165, E250, E300, E350, E410, E450, E550, E600 and E650, with quality sub-classes (A, B, C, BR, D) reflecting impact/notch toughness requirements. Common grades used in Indian construction are E250, E350 and E450, corresponding to the legacy Fe 410W, Fe 490W and Fe 590W designations.

title: IS 2062:2011 - compulsory certification under Quality Control Order
content: Hot Rolled Medium and High Tensile Structural Steel is covered by a Quality Control Order issued by the Ministry of Steel, Government of India, which requires that such steel conform to IS 2062:2011 and be sold only under a valid BIS licence and Standard Mark. Certification for this product is granted under Scheme-I (Schedule-II) of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018.

title: IS 1786:2008 - High Strength Deformed Steel Bars and Wires for Concrete Reinforcement, Specification
content: IS 1786:2008 (fourth revision) covers requirements for deformed steel bars and wires used as reinforcement in concrete, in strength grades Fe415/Fe415D, Fe500/Fe500D, Fe550/Fe550D and Fe600. The number following 'Fe' indicates the specified minimum 0.2 percent proof stress or yield stress in N/mm2, and the letter 'D' denotes a category with the same minimum yield stress but enhanced minimum percentage elongation. The standard also limits chemical composition and carbon equivalent so the material can be readily welded by conventional procedures.

title: IS 1786:2008 - marking and identification requirements for reinforcement bars
content: Under the BIS Product Manual for IS 1786:2008, licensed manufacturers must mark bars or wires during rolling (or by other permanent means) at intervals not exceeding 3 metres, showing the brand name/trade mark, grade of bar/wire, and a six-digit identification number (two digits for the branch office under which the licence operates and the last four digits of the licence number). Certification is granted under Scheme-I of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018.

title: IS 1417:2016 - Gold and Gold Alloys, Jewellery/Artefacts - Fineness and Marking, Specification
content: IS 1417:2016 is the Indian Standard governing the fineness and marking of gold and gold alloy jewellery and artefacts. It permits hallmarking of six caratages (fineness in parts per thousand) of gold jewellery/artefacts: 14K (585), 18K (750), 20K (833), 22K (916), 23K (958) and 24KS (995). Refined gold bars of 995 and 999 fineness produced by BIS-licensed refineries are also marked in accordance with IS 1417:2016.

title: IS 2112:2014 - Silver and Silver Alloys, Jewellery/Artefacts - Fineness and Marking, Specification
content: IS 2112:2014 is the Indian Standard governing the fineness and marking of silver and silver alloy jewellery and artefacts. It permits hallmarking of six grades (fineness in parts per thousand) of silver jewellery/artefacts: 800 (800.0), 835 (835.0), 900 (900.0), 925 (925.0), 970 (970.0) and 990 (990.0).

title: IS 15820:2009 - General Requirements for Establishment and Operation of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres
content: IS 15820:2009 lays down the general requirements for establishing and operating Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs) in India, and is the basis on which BIS grants recognition to AHCs. It also prescribes operational requirements such as the timeframe for returning hallmarked jewellery and cornets to jewellers (within 48 hours).

title: IS 1418:2009 - Determination of Gold by Cupellation (Fire Assay) Method
content: IS 1418:2009 specifies the cupellation (fire assay) method for determination of gold content in gold bullion, gold alloys, and gold jewellery/artefacts. This is the reference method used by Assaying and Hallmarking Centres and BIS referral assay laboratories, including for consumer purity-testing requests, which are chargeable at Rs 200 per article as per BIS's published fee schedule.

title: IS 2113:2014 - Assaying Silver in Silver and Silver Alloys, Methods
content: IS 2113:2014 specifies the methods for assaying (chemically testing the purity of) silver in silver and silver alloys, complementing IS 2112:2014's fineness and marking requirements for silver jewellery and artefacts.

title: IS 17278:2019 - Refined Gold and Silver Bars for Good Delivery, Specification
content: IS 17278:2019 specifies requirements for refined gold and silver bars intended for 'Good Delivery' status, a standard used to assure the quality and traceability of bullion bars produced by refiners for trading purposes, aligning Indian bullion quality practice with international good-delivery norms.

title: IS 9873 (Part 1):2019 - Safety of Toys, non-electric toys
content: IS 9873 (Part 1):2019 is the primary Indian Standard applicable to non-electric toys (ordinary toys such as rattles, dolls, and puzzles that do not have any function dependent on electricity) under India's Toys (Quality Control) Order, 2020. Other parts of IS 9873 (Parts 2, 3, 4, 7 and 9, among others) apply as secondary standards depending on the toy's materials and features.

title: IS 15644:2006 - Safety of Electric Toys
content: IS 15644:2006 is the applicable primary Indian Standard for electric toys - toys that have at least one function dependent on electricity - under the Toys (Quality Control) Order, 2020 issued by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). Manufacturers of electric toys must obtain a separate BIS licence for this category, distinct from non-electric toys covered by IS 9873 (Part 1):2019.

title: Definition of 'Indian Standard' under the BIS Act, 2016
content: Under clause (g) of Section 2 of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, an 'Indian Standard' means the standard, including any tentative or provisional standard, established and published by BIS in relation to any goods, article, process, system or service, indicative of the quality and specification of that goods, article, process, system or service.

title: Standard of the Week / Standard of the Month features
content: BIS publishes a 'Standard of the Week' and 'Standard of the Month' feature on its website to raise public and industry awareness of specific Indian Standards, alongside dashboards listing newly published and recently revised standards, accessible through the BIS website's standards navigation.

title: Download Indian Standards and 'Know Your Standards' portal
content: BIS provides an online portal for purchasing and downloading Indian Standards (standardsbis.bsbedge.com), along with a 'Know Your Standards' facility on the standards.bis.gov.in portal that lets users look up the applicable Indian Standard number for a given product or category, which is also the recommended first step for manufacturers seeking to identify the correct standard before applying for BIS certification.

title: Standardization Cells and Accreditation of Standards Developing Organisations (SDOs)
content: BIS maintains a directory of Standardization Cells and operates a scheme for the Accreditation of Standards Developing Organisations (SDOs), which allows recognized external bodies to participate in or contribute to the standards-development ecosystem in coordination with BIS's technical departments.

title: Standards National Action Plan (SNAP) 2022-27
content: The Standards National Action Plan (SNAP) 2022-27 is BIS's strategic roadmap document intended to serve as a foundation for standardization activity that addresses emerging technologies and sustainability/climate-change concerns, published as a bilingual (English/Hindi) book available on the BIS website.

title: Governing structure: Division Councils cover Ayush, Chemical, Mechanical Engineering, and Management/Systems sectors
content: BIS's standards-formulation activity spans 16 Division Councils covering diverse sectors of the economy and technology, including (among others) Ayush, Chemical, Mechanical Engineering, and Management and Systems, reflecting the breadth of Indian Standards from traditional medicine to modern management-system frameworks.

title: Product Certification Overview - history and purpose
content: BIS's Product Certification scheme traces to the Indian Standards Institution (ISI), established 6 January 1947 as a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, with a mandate to prepare and promote standards for adoption by Indian industry. Today, BIS Product Certification is basically voluntary, allowing manufacturers to obtain a licence to use the ISI Standard Mark on products conforming to the relevant Indian Standard, while a defined set of products are brought under compulsory certification by the Government.

title: Compulsory certification and Quality Control Orders (QCOs)
content: The BIS certification scheme is voluntary in nature, but for a number of products the Central Government makes compliance with the relevant Indian Standard compulsory, citing considerations such as public interest, protection of human, animal or plant health, environmental safety, prevention of unfair trade practices, and national security. For such products, the Government mandates use of the Standard Mark under a licence or Certificate of Conformity (CoC) from BIS, through the issuance of a Quality Control Order (QCO).

title: Overview of BIS certification scheme types (Scheme-I, Scheme-II/CRS, Scheme-IV, Scheme-X, FMCS)
content: BIS operates several conformity-assessment scheme types under the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018: Scheme-I (the standard ISI-mark licence route, applied through QCOs) covering products such as cement, household electrical goods, batteries, chemicals, fertilizers, polymers and textiles; Scheme-II, operated as the Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS) for electronic and IT goods, applied through Compulsory Registration Orders; Scheme-IV (QCO-based) for items such as transformer stampings/laminations/cores and retro-reflective devices for bicycles; Scheme-X for products under the Omnibus Technical Regulation such as low-voltage switchgear and machinery; and the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme (FMCS) for manufacturers located outside India.

title: Product Certification Process - Scheme-I components
content: BIS's Product Certification Process page under Scheme-I addresses: the guideline for grant of licence; guideline for suspension and revocation of suspension of licence; guideline for change in scope of licence; guideline for renewal of licence; guideline for retesting of samples; and guideline for operation of licence, each governing a stage of the licensee's lifecycle with BIS.

title: Essential requirements for obtaining a BIS product licence
content: To obtain a BIS licence, a manufacturer must possess the requisite manufacturing infrastructure, appropriate process controls, and quality-control and testing capability for the product as required by the relevant Indian Standard, and the product itself must conform to all requirements laid down in that Indian Standard. BIS grants the licence after assessing the manufacturer's infrastructure, process controls, quality control, and testing capability through a visit to the manufacturing premises.

title: Meaning of 'licence' under BIS certification
content: A 'licence' under BIS product certification means a licence granted under Section 13 of the BIS Act, 2016 authorizing the licensee to use a specified Standard Mark in relation to goods or articles that conform to the relevant Indian Standard.

title: How to identify the Indian Standard applicable to a product
content: Applicants can search for the Indian Standard applicable to a given product using the licence-related report search on the manakonline.in portal. If the relevant Indian Standard cannot be located this way, applicants are advised to send a query to the concerned technical department of BIS via the technical departments listing on the BIS website.

title: How to apply for a BIS product certification licence
content: Applications for BIS product certification licences are submitted through the online portal www.manakonline.in. Before registering on the portal, applicants are advised to review the applicant user manual and portal FAQs available on the manakonline.in help/important-links section.

title: Product Manuals - technical guidelines for certification
content: BIS publishes 'Product Manuals' as technical guidelines for every product covered under the Product Certification Scheme. A Product Manual includes sampling guidelines, the list of test equipment required, the Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT), and a description of scope, and can be located via Conformity Assessment > Product Certification > Product Specific Guidelines > Product Manuals on the BIS website.

title: Applying for certification of a new product with no existing guidelines
content: If a Product Manual, Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT), grouping guideline, or marking-fee rate does not yet exist for a product, it is likely the applicant is the first manufacturer applying for a BIS licence for that product. Such an applicant can still obtain a BIS licence, following the general principles and procedure for grant of licence set out in Scheme-I of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018.

title: BIS product certification fee components
content: BIS product certification (Scheme-I) fees generally comprise: an application fee to initiate the process; a testing charge to cover conformity testing of the product; an inspection fee (charged per man-day for the factory assessment visit); an annual licence/marking fee to maintain certification validity; a renewal application fee; and an inclusion fee to add further products/varieties to an existing licence. Exact rates vary by product and are set out in each product's Product Manual and marking-fee schedule.

title: List of Products Under Simplified Procedure
content: BIS maintains and publishes a 'List of Products Under Simplified Procedure' - a defined set of products for which BIS offers a faster, less document-intensive certification route compared with the standard Scheme-I process, intended to ease compliance for lower-risk product categories.

title: Testing facilities for product certification - LIMS IS-wise search
content: BIS's Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) portal (lims.bis.gov.in) offers an Indian-Standard-wise search facility allowing applicants and manufacturers to identify which BIS laboratories, BIS-recognized laboratories, or BIS-empanelled laboratories can test a given product against its Indian Standard.

title: FMCS Overview - Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme
content: BIS has operated the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme (FMCS) since the year 2000, under the BIS Act, 2016 and its associated rules and regulations. Under FMCS, a licence is granted to a foreign manufacturer for use of the Standard Mark on a product that conforms to an Indian Standard. The scheme applies to all products except Electronics and IT Goods notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), which fall instead under the Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS). FMCS licences are granted by the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Department (FMCD) at BIS Headquarters, New Delhi.

title: FMCS - Authorized Indian Representative (AIR) requirement
content: Under Scheme-I of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018, foreign manufacturers applying under FMCS who are required to nominate an Indian representative do so via Forms VI and VII; under Scheme-II, the corresponding forms are Form-IIIA, Form-IIIB, and Form-IV. The Authorized Indian Representative (AIR) acts as the manufacturer's point of contact with BIS in India.

title: FMCS - licence validity and renewal
content: Under Scheme-I, BIS certification may be granted initially for up to two years after payment of the advance minimum marking fee. The licence is valid only for the varieties named in it; to extend validity or add further varieties, the licensee must apply with the requisite fee and documents. A licence may be renewed for up to five years from the last date of validity.

title: FMCS contact details
content: Queries relating to the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme can be directed to the FMCS office at Room No. 459, Manakalaya Building, Bureau of Indian Standards, 9 Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg, New Delhi - 110002; telephone 011-2323 0131/3375/9402 or 2360 8280/8319/8449; email fmcs[at]bis[dot]gov[dot]in.

title: Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS) - overview
content: The Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS), operated by BIS through the crsbis.in portal, implements the 'Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement for Compulsory Registration) Order, 2012' notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on 3 October 2012. Under CRS, a manufacturer self-declares that its electronic/IT product conforms to the applicable Indian Standard, backed by testing at a BIS-recognized laboratory, after which BIS issues a registration certificate authorizing use of the Standard Mark with a unique registration (R-) number.

title: CRS - legal and regulatory framework
content: CRS operates as Scheme-II under Annex-II/Schedule-II of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018, made under the BIS Act, 2016. Registration under CRS is based on a manufacturer's self-declaration of conformity, rather than the compulsory factory-inspection model used under Scheme-I product certification; no person may manufacture, import, distribute, sell or store for sale a notified electronics/IT good that does not conform to the specified Indian Standard and does not bear the Standard Mark with a unique registration number.

title: CRS - 'Smart Registration' digital process
content: BIS launched 'Smart Registration' on 3 April 2019 in Delhi - a re-engineered, mobile-compatible, paperless, web-enabled registration process for the Compulsory Registration Scheme, designed to simplify operation and support digital development across the electronics and IT supply chain.

title: CRS - phases and examples of product categories covered
content: CRS product coverage has expanded across several notification phases since October 2012: the initial 2012 order covered 15 electronic items; on 13 November 2014, 15 further items were added including IT-equipment power adaptors, mobile phones, point-of-sale terminals, and copying machines/duplicators; and on 23 August 2017, 13 more items were added including LED floodlights, CCTV cameras/recorders, smart watches, and recessed LED luminaires. CRS-covered standards include IS 13252-1 (IT equipment safety, aligned with IEC 60950-1) and IS 616:2017 (audio-video equipment safety, aligned with IEC 60065).

title: CRS surveillance - role of Software Technology Parks of India (STPI)
content: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has entrusted Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) with administering the surveillance process for the Compulsory Registration Scheme, including random surveillance of registered manufacturers and market surveillance to curb the sale of non-registered or non-compliant notified goods, as well as sample collection/storage/delivery to BIS-recognized laboratories.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards / STPI (surveillance partner)

title: Scheme-X - certification under the Omnibus Technical Regulation
content: BIS's Scheme-X implements compulsory certification under the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018 read with the Omnibus Technical Regulation Order, for machinery and electrical equipment such as low-voltage switchgear and control gear, circuit breakers, switches, motor starters, proximity switches, and emergency-stop devices. Manufacturers must obtain BIS certification and use the Standard Mark for these products, and violations are subject to penalties under the BIS Act, 2016.

title: Scheme-X - other product categories under the Omnibus Technical Regulation
content: Products specifically notified under the Omnibus Technical Regulation (OTR) for Scheme-X certification, per the Ministry of Heavy Industries, include diesel generators (and their assemblies/sub-assemblies), transformers (and their components/parts), power semiconductor converters (and their assemblies), and low-voltage switchgear and control gear.

title: Systems (Management Systems) Certification Scheme - overview
content: BIS has operated a Management Systems Certification Scheme (MSCS) since 1991, initially offering Quality Management System certification (IS/ISO 9001) and gradually expanding to cover other management-system standards. Any organization engaged in manufacture, assembly, or service, with a legal entity in India or abroad, can apply, subject to documents authenticating the organization's name and address. The Management Systems Certification Department at BIS Headquarters, New Delhi is the policy-making body coordinating this activity nationally, in line with ISO/IEC 17021.

title: Systems Certification - management systems currently offered by BIS
content: BIS offers certification against a range of management-system standards, including Quality Management Systems (IS/ISO 9001), Environmental Management Systems (IS/ISO 14001), Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems (IS/ISO 45001), Energy Management Systems (IS/ISO 50001), Anti-Bribery Management Systems (IS/ISO 37001), Information Security Management Systems (IS/ISO 27001), Food Safety Management Systems (IS/ISO 22000), Service Quality Management Systems (IS 15700), Piped Drinking Water Supply/Water Supply Management Systems (IS 17482), Medical Device Quality Management Systems (IS 23485), Social Accountability Management Systems (IS 16001), Road Traffic Safety Management Systems (IS/ISO 39001), and Adventure Tourism Safety Management Systems (IS/ISO 21101).

title: Systems Certification - audit and certification cycle
content: A BIS management-systems certification (licence) is normally granted for three years. The audit programme for initial certification includes a two-stage initial audit, followed by surveillance audits in the first and second years after the certification decision, and a recertification audit in the third year before expiry. Subsequent three-year cycles begin from each recertification decision.

title: Ready Mixed Concrete (RMC) Certification Scheme
content: BIS operates a Ready Mixed Concrete Certification Scheme combining ISO 9001-based process certification with product conformity to IS 4926 (Ready-Mixed Concrete - Code of Practice) for ready-mixed-concrete supplying units, assuring customers of consistent quality concrete at the delivery point; RMC certification may be provided as a standalone process certification or combined with ISO 9001 certification.

title: Integrated Milk Certification Scheme for pasteurized packaged milk
content: BIS's Integrated Milk Certification Scheme combines Food Safety Management System (FSMS) assessment (in line with ISO 22000) - covering a dairy's practices from milk collection at the farmer level through delivery to the retail centre - with product certification (ISI mark) of pasteurized milk pouches against IS 13668, the relevant Indian Standard for packaged pasteurized milk.

title: Toys under compulsory BIS certification
content: Safety of Toys has been under compulsory BIS certification since 1 January 2021, under the Toys (Quality Control) Order, 2020 issued by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Toys are classified as Non-Electric Toys (governed primarily by IS 9873 (Part 1):2019) or Electric Toys (governed primarily by IS 15644:2006); a separate application is required for each toy type, and BIS grants licences under Scheme-I/Scheme-II of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018.

title: Toys certification - support for MSME manufacturers
content: BIS has granted 1,097 licences to domestic toy-manufacturing units, of which 1,061 licences (96.7%) went to Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). BIS has offered concessions in marking fees to micro units, startups, and women entrepreneurs, and initially allowed micro-scale toy manufacturers to obtain a licence without an in-house testing facility for one year - a relaxation later extended to three years in response to the COVID-19 pandemic's effects on industry.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (via Ministry of Consumer Affairs)

title: Penalty for misuse of the BIS Standard Mark - Section 29, BIS Act 2016
content: Under sub-section (2) of Section 29 of the BIS Act, 2016, any person who contravenes sub-sections (6) or (8) of Section 14, or Section 15, is punishable with imprisonment for up to one year, or a fine not less than one lakh rupees (but which may extend up to five times the value of the goods produced, sold, or offered for sale bearing a Standard Mark including Hallmark), or both.

title: Enhanced penalty for repeat/serious violations - Section 29(3), BIS Act 2016
content: Under sub-section (3) of Section 29 of the BIS Act, 2016, contravention of Section 17 is punishable with imprisonment for up to two years, or a fine not less than two lakh rupees for the first contravention and not less than five lakh rupees for a second or subsequent contravention (which may extend up to ten times the value of the goods bearing a Standard Mark, including Hallmark), or both.

title: Compounding of offences under the BIS Act, 2016
content: Under Section 33(1) of the BIS Act, 2016, a first-time offence punishable under the Act (other than one punishable with imprisonment only, or imprisonment and fine) may be compounded, before or after prosecution begins, by an officer authorized by the Director General. The compounding sum cannot exceed the maximum fine that could be imposed under Section 29 for the offence. A subsequent offence occurring more than three years after an earlier compounded offence is treated as a first offence again.

title: Appeals process against BIS orders - Section 34, BIS Act 2016
content: Under Section 34 of the BIS Act, 2016, a person aggrieved by an order made under Section 13, sub-section (4) of Section 14, or Section 17 may appeal to the Director General of BIS within the prescribed period (extendable if sufficient cause is shown). Appeals must be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by a copy of the order appealed against and the prescribed fee, and the appellant must be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard before disposal. A further appeal against certain orders may lie to the Central Government having administrative control of BIS.

title: BIS certification portals by scheme
content: BIS product certification (ISI mark, Scheme-I) and Hallmarking applications are processed through www.manakonline.in, while Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS) applications for electronics and IT goods are processed through www.crsbis.in - the two principal application portals for BIS's main certification and hallmarking activities.

title: BIS Contact for Product Certification enquiries
content: Enquiries relating to product certification applications may be directed to the relevant BIS regional/branch office; for the Central Region this includes branch offices such as Bhopal, Delhi (I and II), Faridabad, Ghaziabad, and Jaipur, with further region-specific contact listings published on the Product Certification Contact Us page of the BIS website.

title: FMCS regulatory basis and Quality Control Orders (QCOs)
content: FMCS is regulated by BIS under the BIS Act, 2016 and the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018. Certification is not mandatory across all product categories; specific goods can be imported into India only with the Standard Mark and a BIS licence once the Government has notified them via a Quality Control Order (QCO). QCOs are issued by relevant ministries under Central Government oversight and published in the Gazette of India, together with their effective date; after that date, no person may manufacture, import, distribute, sell, hire, lease, store, or exhibit for sale a QCO-covered product without a valid licence or Certificate of Conformity and the Standard Mark.

title: BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018 - Scheme framework
content: The BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018, made under the BIS Act, 2016, set out the schedules and schemes (Scheme-I through Scheme-X) that govern how BIS grants, operates, suspends, cancels, and renews certification licences and registrations across product certification, systems certification, hallmarking, and the compulsory registration of electronic/IT goods.

title: ECO Mark scheme for environment-friendly products
content: BIS operates the ECO Mark Scheme, one of its certification programmes, for labelling of environment-friendly products, alongside its Product Certification (ISI mark) and Hallmarking of Gold and Silver Jewellery schemes, as part of its broader conformity-assessment mandate.

title: What is Hallmarking? - definition
content: Hallmarking is the accurate determination and official recording of the proportionate content of precious metal in precious metal articles, as defined with reference to IS 15820. Hallmarks are official marks used in India as a guarantee of the purity or fineness of precious metal articles.

title: Precious metals covered by hallmarking in India
content: At present, two precious metals are brought under the purview of hallmarking in India: gold and silver. Other precious metals are not currently covered by BIS's mandatory or voluntary hallmarking schemes.

title: Objectives of the Hallmarking Scheme
content: The objectives of India's Hallmarking Scheme are to protect consumers against malpractice related to gold and silver purity, to develop India as a leading gold-market centre in the world, and to develop export competitiveness. More broadly, the scheme aims to protect the public against adulteration and to obligate manufacturers to maintain legal standards of fineness.

title: Who operates the Hallmarking Scheme and when it began
content: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Standing Committee on Gold and Precious Metals identified BIS in the year 2000 as the sole agency to operate India's Hallmarking Scheme, entrusting BIS with implementing hallmarking to protect consumers against malpractice and to help make India a leading world market for gold jewellery. BIS operates the scheme nationwide through its network of regional and branch offices. The scheme was aligned with the international Vienna Convention on the Control and Marking of Articles of Precious Metals (1972).

title: BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018 - structure
content: The Bureau of Indian Standards (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018 were notified on 14 June 2018 and are made under the BIS Act, 2016. The Regulations contain three chapters covering: the grant of registration/certification for jewellers; recognition of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs); and the grant of licence for refineries/mints.

title: Hallmarking Regulation 2018 - subsequent amendments
content: The BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018 have been amended multiple times, including amendments notified on 27 October 2021 and 4 March 2022, reflecting the transition of hallmarking from a voluntary to a mandatory scheme and the introduction of the Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) number system.

title: Mandatory Hallmarking Order - original notification
content: The original Mandatory Hallmarking Order was notified on 15 January 2020, marking the Government of India's decision to move gold jewellery and gold artefacts hallmarking from a voluntary to a mandatory regime under the BIS Act, 2016, to be implemented in a phased manner across the country.

title: Mandatory hallmarking - phased rollout amendments and QCO
content: Following the original Mandatory Hallmarking Order (15 Jan 2020), BIS/the Government issued a sequence of amendments extending mandatory coverage: 9 October 2020; 1 June 2021; a Quality Control Order (QCO) dated 23 June 2021 (with published exemption guidelines); 4 April 2022; 3 March 2023; 31 March 2023; 6 September 2023 (adding 55 districts in the third phase); 5 November 2024 (adding 18 districts in the fourth phase); and 31 July 2025 (adding 12 districts in the fifth phase). Later amendments dated 2 March 2026, 28 April 2026 (extending coverage to 385 districts), and 3 August 2026 continued the phased expansion of mandatory hallmarking districts.

title: Introduction of HUID and end of batch-based hallmarking
content: The Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) number was introduced with effect from 1 July 2021, replacing the earlier batch-based hallmarking approach (in which a single hallmark could effectively cover many pieces without individual traceability) with item-level, individually traceable marking of every hallmarked article.

title: What is HUID?
content: HUID stands for Hallmark Unique Identification number - a six-digit alphanumeric number that is unique to each hallmarked item and is traceable. It is one of the three components of a modern hallmark. Consumers can verify a HUID number using the 'Verify HUID' feature of the BIS Care mobile app.

title: Composition of the hallmark on gold jewellery
content: Since the introduction of HUID on 1 July 2021, a hallmark on gold jewellery consists of three marks: the BIS logo (Standard Mark); the purity of the article expressed both in caratage and fineness; and the six-digit alphanumeric HUID number.

title: Permitted gold jewellery caratages/grades under IS 1417:2016
content: IS 1417:2016 permits hallmarking of six caratages (fineness in parts per thousand) of gold jewellery/artefacts: 14K (585), 18K (750), 20K (833), 22K (916), 23K (958) and 24KS (995).

title: Permitted silver jewellery grades under IS 2112:2014
content: IS 2112:2014 permits hallmarking of six grades (fineness in parts per thousand) of silver jewellery/artefacts: 800 (800.0), 835 (835.0), 900 (900.0), 925 (925.0), 970 (970.0) and 990 (990.0).

title: Permissible hallmark size (height) on gold and silver articles
content: BIS specifies permissible heights for the hallmark on precious-metal articles. For gold articles, permitted heights are 1.5 mm, 1.0 mm, 0.75 mm, and 0.5 mm. For silver articles, permitted heights are 4.0 mm, 2.0 mm, 1.5 mm, 1.0 mm, and 0.75 mm, reflecting the different scale considerations for the two metals.

title: Hallmarking of paired articles and detachable parts
content: Each article in a pair, and every detachable part of a piece of jewellery, must carry its own hallmark with a different HUID. Consumers should check the hallmark and fineness details on each individual article or detachable part to guard against misuse of purity claims. A detachable part is any part of jewellery that can be easily removed or replaced.

title: Jewellers Registration Scheme - how to apply
content: A jeweller wishing to obtain a certificate of registration to sell hallmarked gold and silver jewellery/artefacts applies online on the National Single Window System (NSWS) portal (www.nsws.gov.in), which can be accessed directly or via the BIS portal www.manakonline.in. The certificate of registration is granted instantly, without requiring any document upload or fee payment, and remains valid for lifetime.

title: Who must register with BIS as a jeweller
content: Any manufacturer, wholesaler, distributor, or retailer engaged in selling hallmarked precious-metal (gold/silver) articles must mandatorily register with BIS. Artisans/job-workers manufacturing gold jewellery on a job-work basis for jewellers, who are not directly selling to anyone in the supply chain, may be exempted from registration provided they hold supporting documents establishing their status. Jewellers with annual turnover up to Rs 40 lakh do not fall within the purview of mandatory hallmarking, though they may register voluntarily if they wish to sell hallmarked jewellery.

title: Jewellers registration - no fee
content: No fee is charged from jewellers for grant of registration/certification under the Jewellers Registration Scheme; the process is free of cost and the resulting certificate of registration is valid for the jeweller's lifetime.

title: Definition of 'point of sale' for hallmarking responsibility
content: In the chain of Manufacturer, Wholesaler, Distributor, and Retailer, the obligation to get an article hallmarked falls on whichever entity makes the first point of sale, so hallmarking need occur only once. A 'point of sale' is defined as the point at which three conditions are all satisfied: ownership of the article transfers to the purchaser; a valid and compliant tax invoice is generated; and the seller ensures physical delivery of the article to the purchaser.

title: Job work is not treated as a sale for hallmarking purposes
content: Job work performed by an artisan/karigar using gold supplied by the consumer, where the job worker charges only labour charges and ownership of the material remains with the consumer, is not treated as a sale between the consumer and the job worker; consequently, no BIS registration is required for such job work.

title: List of Licensed/Registered Jewellers
content: BIS publishes and maintains a searchable List of Licensed Jewellers on its website, allowing consumers and the public to verify whether a given jewellery retailer, wholesaler, distributor, or manufacturer is BIS-registered before purchasing hallmarked gold or silver jewellery.

title: Assaying and Hallmarking Centre (AHC) - recognition procedure
content: Recognition of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres is based on IS 15820:2009, 'General Requirements for Establishment and Operation of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres'. A centre that has already set up its facility applies to BIS on the prescribed application form, along with a Quality Manual developed on the basis of BIS's Generic Quality Manual, after which BIS assesses the centre's infrastructure, quality management system, and trained/competent manpower before granting recognition.

title: AHC delivery timeframe and delivery voucher content
content: An Assaying and Hallmarking Centre must ensure that hallmarked jewellery/artefacts, together with any retained cornets, are kept ready for delivery back to the client within 48 hours, as required under IS 15820. The AHC's delivery voucher must record: the AHC's name and address; the jeweller's name and address; details of accepted items for hallmarking (weight and quantity per item); details of rejected items; and the weight of the article returned, the weight of the cornet, and the weight of any scrapping.

title: AHC off-site centres
content: An off-site centre is an extended arm of a parent AHC, holding all AHC facilities except fire-assay capability; its liability for malpractice is the same as that of the parent Assaying and Hallmarking Centre. A maximum of five off-site centres, within a 100 km radius, are permitted per parent A&H Centre that has a fire-assay laboratory; off-site centres may be set up both inside and outside mandatory-hallmarking districts.

title: Central assistance/subsidy scheme for setting up AHCs
content: A subsidy of 30% to 75% of the cost of equipment is available under the Government's Central Assistance Scheme for setting up Assaying and Hallmarking Centres at locations deficient in hallmarking infrastructure; the subsidy is not applicable to off-site centres. BIS publishes lists of AHCs that have received central assistance under this scheme.

title: How the digital Assaying & Hallmarking system prevents fraud
content: BIS's Assaying & Hallmarking portal records the date and time of each activity carried out at an AHC, enabling real-time monitoring and calculation of the total time taken from receipt of jewellery through dispatch of the hallmarked item - helping verify that assaying was genuinely performed before laser marking. The introduction of the six-digit HUID number, laser-marked on the jewellery and verifiable through the BIS Care app, further supports authenticity verification and traceability to the responsible jeweller or AHC.

title: AHC obligations - cannot refuse jewellery, must follow FIFO
content: An Assaying and Hallmarking Centre cannot refuse to accept jewellery for hallmarking due to workload or other reasons, though it may inform the jeweller that testing will be delayed; the AHC must follow the First In, First Out (FIFO) principle in processing jewellery it receives.

title: Rejection of non-conforming jewellery by an AHC
content: If jewellery submitted for hallmarking does not conform to the purity declared by the jeweller, the AHC may not hallmark it to a lower grade; instead, the jewellery is rejected and returned to the jeweller. An AHC can likewise return jewellery that does not match the details of purity or weight declared by the jeweller.

title: Gold Refinery/Mint licensing - eligibility and prerequisites
content: Refineries already engaged in gold refining for at least one year, holding accreditation from the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) or National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) accreditation of their laboratory, may apply for a BIS licence to mark the standard bars they produce in accordance with IS 1417:2016 (for 995 and 999 fineness only). Applicants must have in-house manufacturing and testing capability.

title: Gold Refinery licence - scope
content: The scope of a BIS refinery/mint licence covers: gold bullion or gold coin; fineness (999 or 995); and the design and weight of the bullion bar or gold coin, with no negative tolerance permitted on the declared weight. Refinery/mint applications are accepted online only (including payments) via www.manakonline.in.

title: Gold Refinery marking fee
content: The minimum marking fee for gold refinery licensees is Rs 48,000 per annum for large-scale units and Rs 38,400 per annum for MSME units, plus a production-based marking fee of Rs 50 per unit (one unit = one kilogram). At grant of licence, refinery/mint licence validity is one year, and the licence can be renewed for a maximum period of two years.

title: Fee schedule for grant and renewal of licence to refinery or mint
content: BIS's fee schedule for refinery/mint licensing lists: Application Fee Rs 1,000; Licence Fee Rs 1,000; Renewal Application Fee Rs 1,000; Inspection Fee Rs 7,000 per man-day; and Marking Fee (for refined gold per IS 1417) of Rs 48,000 per year minimum for large-scale units and Rs 38,400 per year minimum for MSMEs, at a unit rate of Rs 50 per kilogram. These figures are detailed in Schedule V of the BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018.

title: Fee schedule for recognition of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres
content: BIS's fee schedule for Assaying and Hallmarking Centre (AHC) recognition and renewal lists: Application Fee Rs 10,000; Renewal Application Fee Rs 5,000; Assessment Fee Rs 5,000 per man-day; and Recognition Fee/Renewal of Recognition Fee (valid for three years) Rs 60,000. The assessment fee does not apply to surveillance assessments or complaint investigations.

title: Jeweller registration fee schedule under the 2018 Hallmarking Regulations (historical)
content: Under the original notification implementing the BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018, an application fee of Rs 2,000 was payable with each jeweller registration/renewal application, and a five-year registration fee applied by annual turnover: Rs 80,000 for turnover above Rs 100 crore; Rs 40,000 for turnover above Rs 25 crore and up to Rs 100 crore; Rs 15,000 for turnover above Rs 5 crore and up to Rs 25 crore; and Rs 7,500 for turnover below Rs 5 crore. Jewellers with five or more outlets could opt for a discounted corporate-level registration. This tiered fee structure has since been superseded: current BIS guidance states that jeweller registration is now free of charge and valid for the jeweller's lifetime.

title: Gold Monetization Scheme - role of jewellers, refineries and AHCs
content: Under the Gold Monetization Scheme, BIS publishes lists of jewellers qualifying to act as Collection and Purity Testing Centres (CPTCs), refineries granted licences, and A&H Centres qualifying to act as CPTCs, and periodically invites Expressions of Interest from BIS-registered jewellers and refineries wishing to set up a Collection and Purity Testing Centre under the scheme.

title: Hallmarking charges for gold articles
content: Hallmarking charges for gold articles are Rs 45 per article, with minimum charges for a consignment set at Rs 200 (Service Tax/GST and other applicable levies extra). A 'consignment' is a collection of articles/artefacts of the same fineness from which a sample is drawn and assayed for conformance; a consignment may contain several 'lots', each a set of articles of the same fineness and type/design.

title: Hallmarking charges for silver articles
content: Hallmarking charges for silver articles are Rs 35 per article, with minimum charges for a consignment set at Rs 150 (Service Tax/GST and other applicable levies extra). Hallmarking charges are paid per article irrespective of the weight of the article and do not include making charges or wastage charges.

title: Consumer purity-testing charge at an AHC
content: A common consumer can get hallmarked or unhallmarked jewellery tested for purity at any BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centre, paying a testing charge of Rs 200 for testing by the fire assay method as per IS 1418. The AHC is required to issue an Assay Report giving proper identification details as marked on the article.

title: Compensation to consumers for purity shortfall - Rule 49, BIS Rules 2018
content: Under sub-rule (1) of Rule 49 of the BIS Rules, 2018, where a precious-metal article does not conform to the relevant standard, BIS may direct that compensation payable to the buyer shall be two times the amount of the difference calculated on the basis of the purity shortage for the weight of the article sold, plus the testing charges.

title: BIS complaint registration process for hallmarking issues
content: BIS operates a centralized complaint-redressal procedure through its Complaints Management and Enforcement Department. Complaints can be lodged online through the BIS Care mobile app, the online complaint-registration portal on www.bis.gov.in, or by emailing complaints@bis.gov.in, or offline by contacting/writing to the Public Grievance Officer of the nearest BIS Regional/Branch Office, or directly to the Head of the Complaints Management and Enforcement Department. Complaints received are investigated and further action is taken for redressal.

title: Validity of a hallmark and reselling of hallmarked jewellery
content: The hallmark on jewellery is valid for the entire lifetime of the hallmarked article. Consumers may also sell old, unhallmarked or already-hallmarked jewellery back to jewellers; and a hallmark remains valid even if the jewellery is returned to the jeweller by a customer after being sold.

title: BIS Care app - Verify HUID and jeweller identification
content: A consumer can identify the jeweller's name and registration number associated with a piece of hallmarked jewellery by using the 'Verify HUID' feature of the BIS Care mobile app, entering the six-digit HUID number laser-marked on the article to retrieve details such as the jeweller's registration number, purity, and hallmarking date.

title: Exemptions from mandatory hallmarking under the Quality Control Order
content: Under the Quality Control Order for mandatory gold-jewellery hallmarking, the following are exempt: articles for export that conform to a foreign buyer's specification; articles weighing less than two grams; articles in transit from outside India to a recognized AHC for hallmarking; articles for medical, dental, veterinary, scientific, or industrial use; gold thread articles; manufactured articles that are not 'substantially complete' and are intended for further manufacture; gold bullion in bar/plate/sheet/foil/rod/wire/strip/tube/coin form; articles for export-and-reimport under Government trade policy; jewellery for international exhibitions; jewellery for approved domestic B2B exhibitions; special-category jewellery (Kundan, Polki, and Jadaau); jewellers with annual turnover up to Rs 40 lakh; and gold watches and fountain pens.

title: Definition of 'substantially complete' under the hallmarking QCO
content: Under the Quality Control Order for hallmarking, a manufactured article that is not intended for further manufacture is treated as 'substantially complete' for the purposes of the exemption for articles not yet substantially complete.

title: Hallmarking of jewellery weighing less than 2 grams
content: Jewellery weighing under 2 grams (or with detachable parts under 2 grams) is exempt from mandatory hallmarking, reflecting the practical difficulty of marking very small or intricately designed pieces. However, if the jeweller wishes, such articles may still be hallmarked by an AHC after testing under IS 1418.

title: Re-hallmarking requirement for pre-HUID hallmarked jewellery
content: Jewellery that was hallmarked before the six-digit HUID system was introduced must be re-hallmarked (either adding the HUID alongside existing marks, or erasing existing marks as the jeweller prefers) before it can be sold, per amendments to the Mandatory Hallmarking Order dated 3 March 2023 and 31 March 2023. Jewellery that is re-hallmarked after being subject to the full assaying process, and found conforming, can also be re-hallmarked if the original hallmarked portion is damaged or erased.

title: Melting and re-hallmarking of jewellery
content: A jeweller may melt an old piece of jewellery already hallmarked with a six-digit HUID to make new jewellery, and get the new item hallmarked with a fresh HUID before selling it. As of the relevant BIS guidance, a provision to deactivate or disable the original HUID upon melting is under development and not yet in place.

title: White gold and gold-alloy coverage under mandatory hallmarking
content: White gold alloy is covered under mandatory hallmarking. More generally, if an alloy made by mixing gold with one or more other metals conforms to a grade specified under IS 1417, the resulting article is covered by mandatory hallmarking.

title: Hallmarking of imported jewellery
content: Jewellery may be imported into India, but it can only be sold by a registered jeweller after it is tested and hallmarked by a BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centre; jewellery already hallmarked under an exporting country's own provisions must still be re-hallmarked in India.

title: Gold bullion and coins are not covered by the mandatory jewellery hallmarking order
content: The Mandatory Hallmarking Order applies only to gold jewellery and gold artefacts, not to gold bullion or coins. Gold bullion/coins of 999/995 fineness may only be hallmarked by BIS-approved refineries/mints - as of 31 July 2023, 46 refineries were licensed and operating for this purpose, with the list of BIS-licensed refineries/mints published on the BIS website.

title: Jeweller liability for purity/fineness of hallmarked jewellery
content: Under BIS Hallmarking Regulations, the registered jeweller who gets an article hallmarked is responsible for the purity and fineness of that article, and the registered jeweller who makes the sale is liable to pay compensation for any shortage in purity or fineness, as per applicable rules.

title: Cancellation of a jeweller's certificate of registration - grounds
content: Under Regulation 7 of the BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018, BIS may cancel a jeweller's certificate of registration if: any declaration made by the jeweller is found false or incorrect; the jeweller has violated any term or condition of the certificate; the jeweller has sold or offered for sale a hallmarked article of purity/fineness lower than claimed or marked; the jeweller has failed to cooperate with BIS's authorised representative during a surveillance visit or complaint investigation; or the jeweller is found indulging in unfair practices amounting to misuse of the hallmark.

title: Procedure for cancellation of a jeweller's certificate of registration
content: Under Regulation 7 of the BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018: before cancelling a certificate of registration, BIS gives notice to the jeweller of its intention to cancel, citing reasons; the jeweller may submit an explanation within 14 days of receiving the notice; BIS may consider the explanation and grant a personal hearing; if the offence is compounded, the certificate is not processed for cancellation; and if no explanation is submitted, BIS may cancel the certificate on expiry of the notice period.

title: Who bears penal liability for a failed hallmarked sample
content: Among the Manufacturer, Wholesaler, Distributor, and Retailer, whichever entity had the article hallmarked bears responsibility for penal action if a hallmarked sample fails on retesting. The Assaying and Hallmarking Centre that hallmarked the article is equally responsible for penal action in the case of a failed sample; the jeweller and AHC are jointly liable to be proceeded against in cases of deficient purity.

title: AHC compensation liability for purity shortfall - Section 18(7), BIS Act 2016
content: Under Section 18(7) of the BIS Act, 2016, where a certified body or licence holder (or its representative) has sold Standard-Marked goods, articles, processes, systems, or services that do not conform to the relevant standard, BIS may direct the certified body/licence holder to repair, replace, or reprocess the item, or to pay compensation to the consumer as prescribed. Under Rule 49(1) of the BIS Rules, 2018, that compensation for a non-conforming precious-metal article is two times the amount of the purity-difference calculated for the weight of the article sold, plus the testing charges.
clause: Section 18(7), BIS Act 2016; Rule 49(1), BIS Rules 2018

title: Multi-caratage jewellery hallmarking (e.g., necklace with a different-grade chain)
content: Where a jewellery item is made using multiple parts of different caratages - for example, a necklace of 22K joined to a back chain of 14K - since each part is manufactured separately (whether detachable or permanently joined), each part must be hallmarked separately with its own hallmark and HUID.

title: Responsibility for adulterated bullion reaching a jeweller unknowingly
content: Hallmarking of gold bullion by BIS-licensed refineries is voluntary; if hallmarked bullion later fails testing, a complaint may be made to BIS. If bullion is un-hallmarked, responsibility for ensuring the resulting jewellery's purity lies with the jeweller. If jewellery made from such bullion is found non-conforming at an AHC, it is returned to the jeweller rather than hallmarked.

title: Antique/heirloom jewellery and non-standard caratages
content: Any jewellery sold in a mandatory-hallmarking district must be hallmarked according to the grades specified in IS 1417, even antique or heirloom pieces, though such jewellery can be hallmarked at the next-lower grade/fineness permitted under IS 1417 if it does not exactly match one of the six standard caratages. BIS notes that around two years were given for jewellers to clear old, un-hallmarked stock before mandatory hallmarking took full effect.

title: Bill/invoice requirements for hallmarked jewellery sales
content: A jeweller's bill or invoice for a hallmarked precious-metal article must separately indicate the description of each article, the net weight of the precious metal, the purity in carat and fineness, and the hallmarking charges. It is necessary for consumers to obtain an authentic bill/invoice for a hallmarked article, since these details are required for any future dispute, misuse claim, or complaint redressal. However, mentioning the HUID number on the invoice is currently voluntary, and jewellers are not required to maintain a record of HUID numbers.

title: Consumer checklist when purchasing hallmarked jewellery
content: At a registered/certified jeweller's outlet, the shop should display the BIS logo with the wording 'Hallmarked jewellery available for sale' on the outside, and should display its certificate of registration inside the shop. The jeweller must have a magnifying glass of at least 10X magnification to show the hallmark to customers, and the relationship between caratage and fineness should be displayed in the shop.

title: BIS surveillance of registered jewellers and AHCs
content: BIS carries out regular surveillance audits of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres and draws market samples from registered/certified jewellers for testing in BIS's referral assay laboratories (RALs), as part of its ongoing quality control over the hallmarking ecosystem.

title: Only registered jewellers may approach an AHC for hallmarking
content: An artisan or member of the public cannot directly approach an Assaying and Hallmarking Centre for hallmarking of jewellery; only BIS-registered/certified jewellers may submit jewellery to an AHC for hallmarking.

title: Sending jewellery to an AHC via the Manakonline portal
content: To send jewellery to an Assaying and Hallmarking Centre through the portal, a jeweller logs into www.manakonline.in, selects the 'Hallmarking' tile, logs in with username and password, clicks 'New Request' to generate a request, selects the AHC, and fills in details such as item category, quantity, item category weight, and declared purity in the 'Jeweller's Hallmarking Request' page before submitting to the AHC. Provision also exists for the AHC to initiate a hallmarking request on the jeweller's behalf without the jeweller using the portal directly.

title: Alteration limits for hallmarked jewellery
content: Jewellers are permitted to make alterations to hallmarked jewellery of up to 2 grams, or 50% of the article's weight, whichever is lower, without needing to re-hallmark. As of the relevant guidance, the online hallmarking system had no provision to reflect such alterations; if a customer requests an alteration beyond the permitted limit in a non-mandatory district and wants the jewellery hallmarked, the article must be re-hallmarked at a nearby BIS-recognized AHC.

title: Transferring hallmarked jewellery stock between a jeweller's own outlets
content: If a BIS-registered jeweller transfers jewellery stock between its own inter- or intra-company sales outlets under the same PAN number (i.e., no sale is occurring), hallmarking is not required for that transfer, provided proper documentation of the transfer is maintained.

title: Business-to-business exhibition and export exemptions
content: Under the Mandatory Hallmarking Order dated 23 June 2021, jewellery being transported for approved domestic business-to-business exhibitions is exempt from mandatory hallmarking, as are certain export- and exhibition-related movements of un-hallmarked jewellery; detailed guidance on these exemptions is published by BIS in a dedicated exemptions document.

title: Marks that may legally appear on hallmarked jewellery
content: On hallmarked jewellery, three marks are mandatory: the BIS Standard Mark (BIS logo); the purity in carat and fineness; and the six-digit HUID number. Beyond these mandatory marks, a manufacturer or jeweller may also add their own mark to hallmarked jewellery/artefacts.

title: Jeweller cooperation obligations during BIS surveillance visits
content: A registered/certified jeweller must cooperate with BIS representatives visiting the outlet for surveillance, including permitting the collection of samples of hallmarked gold/silver jewellery/artefacts available for sale, which are then used to verify conformity with the relevant Indian Standard, including the marked fineness.

title: Complaint redressal procedure between consumer, jeweller and AHC
content: A customer can directly approach the jeweller for compensation if hallmarked jewellery, when retested at any BIS-recognized AHC, is found to be of lower purity than declared. If a complaint is instead made to BIS, BIS follows a defined complaint-redressal procedure involving investigation at both the complainant's end and the accused's end (including registered jewellers and the AHC), with any action taken only after a thorough investigation, in accordance with the BIS Act, 2016 and the Hallmarking Regulations.

title: Contact details - Deputy Director General (Hallmarking)
content: Enquiries relating to Hallmarking can be directed to the office of DDG (Hallmarking), Room No. 555 [also listed elsewhere as Room No. 410], Manakalaya, Bureau of Indian Standards, 9 Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg, New Delhi - 110002; telephone 011-23234223 (Ext. 8368) or 011-23233650; email hallmarking[at]bis[dot]gov[dot]in or ddghallmarking[at]bis[dot]gov[dot]in.

title: Phased district coverage under mandatory hallmarking
content: Mandatory hallmarking of gold jewellery has been rolled out across India in successive phases, with BIS periodically publishing lists of additional districts brought under the mandatory order - including an addition of 55 districts in the third phase (2023), 18 districts in the fourth phase (2024), and 12 districts in the fifth phase (2025) - alongside a broader phase-wise coverage document tracking cumulative district coverage, which by an April 2026 amendment extended to 385 districts.

title: Vienna Convention alignment of India's hallmarking scheme
content: India's BIS Hallmarking Scheme has been aligned with international criteria on hallmarking under the Vienna Convention (1972) on the Control and Marking of Articles of Precious Metal, reflecting BIS's intent to bring Indian hallmarking practice in line with globally recognized standards even though India is not a full contracting party operating a Common Control Mark under that convention.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (via Invest India archive)

title: Summary of Indian Standards underpinning the Hallmarking Scheme
content: India's hallmarking scheme rests on a defined set of Indian Standards: IS 1417:2016 (gold fineness and marking), IS 2112:2014 (silver fineness and marking), IS 15820:2009 (requirements for Assaying and Hallmarking Centres), IS 1418:2009 (cupellation/fire-assay method for gold), IS 2113:2014 (methods for assaying silver), and IS 17278:2019 (refined gold and silver bars for Good Delivery).

title: Benefits of hallmarking to consumers and jewellers
content: Hallmarked jewellery provides third-party assurance to a customer that they are getting the right purity of gold/silver for the price paid (value for money). For jewellers, obtaining BIS registration/certification provides a clear indication of their capability and strong evidence of their commitment to quality and consistency in the purity of the gold/silver jewellery they sell.

title: Where to find hallmarking information and lists of registered entities
content: All detailed information on hallmarking - including general information, the Hallmarking Regulation, Mandatory Hallmarking Orders, procedures and guidelines for jewellers and hallmarking centres, forms, and lists of registered jewellers and recognized hallmarking centres - is available on the BIS website under the Hallmarking section, with the list of BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres also accessible via manakonline.in.

title: BIS Laboratory Services - overview
content: To protect consumer interests, BIS operates various conformity-assessment schemes under which it grants licences/registrations to manufacturers capable of producing goods that conform to relevant Indian Standards on a continuous basis. To support these schemes, which require regular testing of products for conformity, BIS has established a network of eight laboratories across the country.

title: History of BIS's laboratory network
content: BIS's laboratory network began with the establishment of a Central Laboratory at Sahibabad in 1962. BIS subsequently added four Regional Laboratories at Mohali, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai, and five Branch Laboratories at Patna, Bangalore (Bengaluru), Guwahati, Jammu and Hyderabad, giving BIS its present-day network of laboratories for conformity-assessment testing.

title: Testing disciplines covered by BIS laboratories
content: BIS laboratories have testing facilities covering chemical, microbiological, electrical, and mechanical requirements of products. In addition to general product testing, BIS has established Gold jewellery testing laboratories at nine of its laboratories; the Regional Laboratory at Chennai also tests silver jewellery.

title: NABL accreditation of BIS laboratories
content: To demonstrate commitment to quality and keep pace with national and international good laboratory practices, BIS laboratories at Sahibabad, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Mohali, Bengaluru, Patna and Guwahati have been accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) as per ISO/IEC 17025.

title: Laboratory Recognition Scheme (LRS) - outside laboratories
content: To meet the rising need for testing under its conformity-assessment schemes, BIS also operates a Laboratory Recognition Scheme (LRS), recognizing outside laboratories where it is not economically viable for BIS to build its own test facilities, or where there is a large inflow of samples. The scheme is based on ISO/IEC 17025, in line with NABL norms. BIS has recognized 293 such laboratories, including reputed R&D organizations, technical institutions, government laboratories, and private-sector laboratories.

title: Laboratory Recognition Scheme amendments
content: The Laboratory Recognition Scheme governing BIS's recognition and empanelment of outside laboratories has been updated through subsequent amendments, including a Laboratory Recognition Scheme Amendment 2020 and a Laboratory Recognition Scheme Amendment 2022, both published on the BIS website alongside the original scheme document.

title: Group-1 and Group-2 laboratory categories
content: BIS categorizes outside laboratories used for its conformity-assessment testing into Group-1 (BIS-recognized laboratories, recognized under the Laboratory Recognition Scheme) and Group-2 (government laboratories empanelled by BIS). BIS publishes separate lists for Group-1 recognized laboratories and Group-2 empanelled laboratories on its website, along with lists of NABL-, QAI-, FDAS-, and IQAS-accredited laboratories used in specific schemes.

content: The BIS Eastern Regional Laboratory (ERL) is located at P-230, CIT Scheme, VII-M, Block-W, Kankurgachi, Kolkata - 700054 (Annex Building & Sample Cell), with a Main Building at 1/14, CIT Scheme VII M, VIP Road, Kankurgachi, Kolkata - 700054, West Bengal. Contact: sample.erol@bis.gov.in; telephone +91 33 23209474 / 23208561.

title: BIS, Northern Regional Laboratory (NRL) - Mohali
content: The BIS Northern Regional Laboratory (NRL) is located at B-69, Industrial Focal Point, Phase VII, Mohali, S.A.S. Nagar, Punjab - 160059. Contact: nrol@bis.gov.in; telephone +91 172 4802676.

title: BIS, Southern Regional Laboratory (SRL) - Chennai
content: The BIS Southern Regional Laboratory (SRL) is located at IV Cross Road, CIT Campus, Taramani, Chennai - 600113, Tamil Nadu. Contact: srol@bis.gov.in; telephone +91 44 22541208. The Chennai regional laboratory is notable for also carrying out silver jewellery testing in addition to gold.

title: BIS, Western Regional Laboratory (WRL) - Mumbai
content: The BIS Western Regional Laboratory (WRL) is located at Plot No. E9, Road No. 8, M.I.D.C, Andheri (East), Mumbai, Maharashtra - 400093. Contact: wrol@bis.gov.in; telephone +91 22 28329295.
