title: Withdrawal of QCOs for six industrial chemicals (November 2025)
content: On 20 November 2025, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers rescinded six Quality Control Orders with immediate effect, covering Pyridine and Beta Picoline (originally under 2020 QCOs), Sodium Tripolyphosphate (2020 QCO), and H Acid, K Acid, and Vinyl Sulphone (originally under 2024 QCOs) - illustrating that BIS's mandatory-certification landscape for industrial chemicals is actively reviewed and can contract as well as expand over time.

title: Postponement of QCO implementation dates for compliance-time relief
content: Ministries administering QCOs periodically postpone implementation/compliance dates via Gazette notification to give affected manufacturers more preparation time - for example, the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals postponed three textile-related QCOs in a notification dated 5 January 2026, and separately postponed the compliance date for the HDPE/PP Woven Sacks for Packaging Fertilizers QCO to 6 September 2024 via a notification dated 4 June 2024.

title: India eliminates mandatory BIS certification for six key chemicals (November 2025)
content: On 20 November 2025, the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals (DCPC), Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, issued notifications withdrawing six previously mandatory Quality Control Orders for industrial chemicals, based on public-interest considerations and in consultation with BIS - part of a broader deregulatory review of chemical-sector QCOs undertaken by the ministry in late 2025.

title: Testing-charge variability across BIS-certified product categories
content: Testing charges under BIS product certification vary substantially by product, reflecting the complexity and cost of the required tests - for example, published per-clause testing-charge breakups for products such as electrical appliances (IS 302 Part 1) and lithium-ion batteries (IS 16046 Part 2) show individual test-line charges ranging from a few hundred rupees to tens of thousands of rupees, with total product testing costs that can run from tens of thousands to several lakh rupees depending on the product and the laboratory.

title: BIS Talks - product-specific educational video series supporting certification awareness
content: BIS publishes a series of short educational videos, 'BIS Talks', covering specific certified-product categories - including LPG cylinders, domestic pressure cookers, packed drinking water, Portland Slag Cement, Ordinary Portland Cement, PVC-insulated cables, pressed ceramic tiles, safety footwear, and mixer grinders - explaining how Indian Standards are applied at each stage of manufacturing, from raw-material selection through intermediate quality checks to final destructive/non-destructive testing.

title: Products certified under multiple/overlapping regulatory regimes
content: Some product categories require compliance with both BIS certification and another regulator's approval before sale in India - for example, LPG cylinders and their valve fittings, which fall under BIS Standard Mark certification (IS 3196 series, IS 8737) while related transport/storage safety aspects of compressed and liquefiable gases in India are also overseen by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), reflecting that BIS certification can sit alongside, rather than replace, other sector-specific regulatory approvals.

title: Certification schemes summary table - ISI Mark, Hallmark, CRS, ECO Mark, FMCS
content: BIS's certification landscape spans five broad scheme families, each with a distinct application portal and process: the ISI Mark (Scheme-I product certification, for general goods under QCOs); BIS Hallmark (gold/silver jewellery, via manakonline.in); the Compulsory Registration Scheme/CRS (electronics and IT goods, via crsbis.in); the ECO Mark (environment-friendly products); and the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme/FMCS (for manufacturers based outside India, for products other than Electronics/IT goods) - together covering several hundred product categories under compulsory certification as of the mid-2020s.

title: Number and regional distribution of recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres
content: BIS has recognized a large network of gold Assaying and Hallmarking facilities across India - reported at 923 centres in one CPCB compilation - with the Southern region hosting the highest concentration (312 centres), followed by the Western region (203), Eastern region (181), Central region (133), and Northern region (94), reflecting the concentration of India's jewellery manufacturing and retail hubs.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (via Maharashtra Pollution Control Board)

title: Gold assaying process at an AHC - reception, XRF screening, and sample preparation
content: The gold-assaying process at a BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centre generally follows defined stages: a Reception Section where items are logged and matched against the jeweller's declaration; a non-destructive X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Section, where items are screened quickly to identify constituent metals and decide which parts need closer testing; and, where destructive confirmatory testing is needed, a Melting Section where small sampled portions are cut/drilled and melted together to form a homogeneous sample for further analysis.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (via Maharashtra Pollution Control Board)

title: XRF versus fire-assay (cupellation) testing methods compared
content: Two principal testing methods are used in India's hallmarking ecosystem: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF), a modern, non-destructive, quick, and computer-automated technique typically used to screen finished gold articles and print the hallmark; and the fire-assay (cupellation) method under IS 1418:2009, in which the article is melted to separate gold from impurities - a more time-consuming, destructive, but highly accurate method commonly used for raw gold, bullion, and confirmatory/referee testing, including consumer purity-testing requests and dispute resolution.

title: AHC equipment requirements - XRF machine, laser marking machine, and software integration
content: Per BIS guidance for Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, an AHC must have equipment capable of supporting the centralized AHC software's full functionality, including calibration of equipment (through a NABL-accredited laboratory, or otherwise traceable to national standards) and use of Certified Reference Materials (CRMs, sourced from an Indian Government Mint or a NABL-accredited laboratory) to check the XRF machine. XRF machines and laser marking machines used for hallmarking must have built-in software enabling direct, real-time data transfer to BIS's centralized Assaying & Hallmarking software for operational monitoring.

title: AHC premises and infrastructure requirements
content: Per general guidance for setting up an Assaying and Hallmarking Centre under IS 15820, minimum premises requirements typically include at least 600 sq ft of total space (with the assaying laboratory occupying a minimum of 150 sq ft), uninterrupted power supply supplemented by a diesel generator (commonly around 15 kVA backup capacity), air-conditioning, and safety infrastructure such as CCTV surveillance and secure lockers for precious-metal storage, in addition to the layout requirements specified by BIS.

title: Certified Reference Materials (CRMs) for AHC equipment verification
content: Assaying and Hallmarking Centres are required to use Certified Reference Materials (CRMs) with purity certificates issued by an Indian Government Mint or a NABL-accredited laboratory to check and verify the accuracy of their XRF machines, ensuring that non-destructive screening results remain traceable to nationally recognized purity standards over the equipment's operating life.

title: Environmental concerns with the fire-assay method and CPCB guidelines
content: The fire-assay method, while a globally used and highly accurate analytical technique, releases toxic lead fumes as a by-product, raising environmental and occupational-health concerns. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has issued environmental guidelines (following orders of the National Green Tribunal) covering the modalities for environmental clearance of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres using the fire-assay method, prompting the hallmarking industry to explore cleaner, 'greener' alternative approaches to gold purity testing without compromising accuracy.

title: On-Site Centres (OSC) - guidelines for AHC-affiliated satellite testing points
content: BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs) may set up On-Site Centres (OSCs), also referred to as off-site centres, as satellite testing points offering all AHC facilities except fire-assay testing (which remains the responsibility of the parent AHC). A parent AHC may establish a maximum of five OSCs within a 100 km radius, generally intended to extend hallmarking access to districts not already covered by dedicated hallmarking infrastructure, subject to application and approval by the relevant BIS Regional Office.

title: BIS Hallmarking Scheme 2005 - historical procedure for AHC recognition
content: Before the current online recognition process, BIS's 'Procedure for According Recognition/Renewal of Recognition to the Assaying & Hall Marking Centres' (document HM/AHC/P-2, October 2005) governed recognition under the 'BIS Hallmarking Scheme 2005', requiring a centre to have independent legal identity with no ownership linkage to jewellers/artefact manufacturers/retailers (though the centre could be run by a jewellers'/manufacturers' association), and to submit a formal application with prescribed fees, illustrating the scheme's procedural evolution over nearly two decades to today's IS 15820:2009-based, portal-driven recognition process.

title: AHC recognition for silver hallmarking - basis in IS 2113
content: Recognition of an Assaying and Hallmarking Centre to certify silver and silver alloy jewellery/artefacts is generally considered for centres offering complete testing per IS 2113 (Assaying Silver in Silver and Silver Alloys, Methods), alongside BIS's general criteria for hallmarking recognition - meaning a centre wishing to hallmark silver, not just gold, must demonstrate full silver-assaying and hallmarking facilities as a distinct capability from gold hallmarking.

title: Documents typically required to apply for AHC recognition
content: An applicant seeking BIS recognition as an Assaying and Hallmarking Centre typically needs to submit self-certified copies of documents including: premises documents; Udyog Aadhaar/MSME registration; CA certificate and GST registration; partnership deed or Memorandum of Association; identity proof of top management; staff qualification certificates and identity documents; equipment calibration certificates; Certified Reference Material (CRM) certificates; an insurance policy; Inter-Laboratory Comparison (ILC) reports; and in-house test reports for water and nitric acid used in the assaying process.

title: AHC recognition applications are submitted to the jurisdictional BIS Regional Office
content: An applicant AHC submits its self-certified application documents to the Regional Office of BIS having jurisdiction over the area where the Assaying and Hallmarking Centre is located, rather than to BIS Headquarters directly, reflecting BIS's decentralized regional-office structure for hallmarking-centre recognition and ongoing oversight.

title: Laser marking of HUID - non-destructive, automated printing
content: Once an article's purity has been determined (via XRF screening or fire assay), the HUID hallmark - comprising the BIS logo, purity/fineness, and the six-digit alphanumeric HUID - is applied to finished jewellery using laser marking equipment, which prints the hallmark in a non-destructive, computer-automated manner directly linked to BIS's centralized Assaying & Hallmarking software for real-time record-keeping and traceability.

title: Options for consumers when no local AHC is available
content: Where a consumer's locality has no nearby BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centre, purity-testing or complaint-related needs can still be addressed by approaching the nearest BIS Regional or Branch Office, using the BIS Care app's online complaint and verification features, or contacting BIS's central Hallmarking division directly, since BIS's regulatory oversight and complaint-redressal functions are not limited to areas with a physically co-located AHC.

title: Hallmark validity versus a jeweller's own warranty or guarantee
content: The BIS hallmark itself is a third-party purity certification valid for the lifetime of the article and is distinct from any separate warranty or buy-back guarantee a jeweller may voluntarily offer on a piece of jewellery (such as a making-charge waiver on exchange, or a lifetime exchange policy) - the hallmark addresses purity assurance, while commercial warranties address other aspects of the purchase and are matters of contract between the jeweller and the consumer.

title: Gold coins sold by banks are generally outside the mandatory jewellery hallmarking order
content: Gold coins sold by banks are typically imported bullion products rather than jewellery/artefacts manufactured or sold by a registered jeweller in the retail jewellery supply chain, so they generally fall outside the scope of the Mandatory Hallmarking Order for gold jewellery and artefacts; such coins may instead be marked under refinery/mint provisions of IS 1417:2016 where the issuing refinery holds a BIS licence, but consumers should verify purity/fineness marks specific to the product they are purchasing rather than assume jewellery-hallmarking rules automatically apply.

title: World Standards Day outreach on hallmarking
content: BIS uses World Standards Day (14 October) and similar outreach occasions - such as its 'BIS Talks on LPG Cylinder' video, produced for a World Standards Day celebration by the BIS Ahmedabad Branch Office - to raise public awareness of Indian Standards relevant to daily life, including standards underpinning consumer-facing certification and hallmarking activities.

title: BIS Talks video series - hallmarking-adjacent educational content
content: BIS's 'BIS Talks' educational video series, while primarily focused on general product certification, sits alongside dedicated hallmarking-specific outreach material; the broader series includes topics like 'BIS First' (highlighting BIS's various pioneering initiatives), reflecting BIS's multi-channel approach - webpages, FAQs, guidelines, apps, and video content - to making its certification, standards, and hallmarking information accessible to manufacturers, jewellers, and consumers alike.

title: Hallmarking's role in developing India as a global gold-trading hub
content: One of the stated objectives behind BIS being entrusted with hallmarking in 2000 was to help develop India as a leading centre for the world gold market and to develop export competitiveness for Indian gold jewellery - a policy objective distinct from, but complementary to, the scheme's core consumer-protection purpose of preventing purity-related malpractice in the domestic jewellery trade.

title: BIS hallmarking guideline document numbering convention
content: BIS's internal hallmarking guideline and procedure documents follow a structured reference-numbering convention, such as 'HM/A&HC/Guidelines/2, September 2018' (for AHC recognition and operation guidelines) or 'HM/AHC/P-2, October 2005' (for the earlier AHC recognition procedure) - identifying the subject area (Hallmarking, Assaying & Hallmarking Centre), document type (Guidelines, Procedure), and a running number and issue date, useful for tracing the specific version of a hallmarking guideline referenced in older correspondence or compliance documentation.

title: Common governance thread across recognition, renewal, suspension and cancellation of AHC recognition
content: BIS's guideline documents for Assaying and Hallmarking Centres address the centre's full regulatory lifecycle under a common framework - covering the procedures for grant of recognition, renewal of recognition, and suspension or cancellation of recognition - paralleling the equivalent lifecycle guidelines (grant, renewal, suspension/revocation, change in scope) that BIS applies to product-certification licensees under Scheme-I.

title: Silver hallmarking has historically seen lower adoption than gold hallmarking
content: While gold hallmarking has moved through phased mandatory rollout since 2021, silver hallmarking under IS 2112:2014 has generally remained on a more limited, largely need-based recognition footing for Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (an AHC must separately demonstrate IS 2113-based silver-testing capability to be recognized for silver), reflecting a comparatively slower pace of mandatory-coverage expansion for silver relative to gold within India's hallmarking programme.

title: AHC set-up sequence - from preparation through audit to licence grant
content: Setting up a new Assaying and Hallmarking Centre generally follows a defined sequence: basic preparation of the centre per IS 15820 (premises, staffing, XRF and laser-marking equipment procurement); in-house set-up of the assaying laboratory; training of the Assay Master to BIS norms; preparation of supporting documentation (Inter-Laboratory Comparison reports, Certified Reference Material certificates, insurance); submission of the recognition application to the jurisdictional BIS Regional Office; testing of a CRM sample from a BIS-recognized laboratory; an audit by BIS's competent authority; and, upon successful completion, grant of recognition, followed by ongoing annual maintenance and staff training on record-keeping, marking, and use of the BIS hallmarking portal.

title: Illustrative cost components for setting up an AHC
content: Setting up a new Assaying and Hallmarking Centre involves both BIS regulatory fees and separate infrastructure costs: BIS-side fees generally include an application-and-assessment charge and a recognition fee (valid for three years), while infrastructure costs - such as the XRF machine, laser marking machine, and weighing balances - are borne separately by the applicant and are not part of BIS's own fee schedule, meaning total AHC set-up cost varies considerably based on equipment vendor and premises fit-out choices.

title: Hallmarking's place within BIS's broader quality-infrastructure mandate
content: Hallmarking is one of five core pillars of BIS's mandate alongside standards formulation, product certification, laboratory recognition, and consumer engagement - and is distinguished from BIS's other certification schemes by being centred on a single, high-value consumer-goods category (gold and silver jewellery/artefacts) with its own dedicated regulatory chapter (the BIS Hallmarking Regulations, 2018), its own online portal workflow, its own fee schedule, and its own network of specialized testing infrastructure (Assaying and Hallmarking Centres) distinct from BIS's general product-testing laboratory network.

title: Standard of the Week - Bureau of Indian Standards
content:
Standard of the Week
IS 19873: 2026 / ISO 21087: 2019
Gas Analysis — Analytical Methods for Hydrogen Fuel — Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) Fuel Cell Applications for Road Vehicles
This Indian Standard, identical to ISO 21087:2019, specifies the validation protocol for analytical methods used to ensure the quality of gaseous hydrogen supplied at hydrogen distribution bases and refuelling stations for road vehicles using proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells. It complements existing standards such as IS 16061/ISO 14687, which sets hydrogen fuel quality specifications, and IS 18538-8/ISO 19880-8, which covers quality assurance protocols, by providing the analytical methodology needed to measure contaminant levels in hydrogen fuel to grade D purity requirements.
This defines key performance characteristics that any analytical method must satisfy before being used for quality control, including selectivity, limit of detection, limit of quantification, working range, trueness (bias and recovery), precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and reproducibility), measurement uncertainty, and ruggedness. For each characteristic, it prescribes fitness-for-purpose criteria, generally requiring a relative combined standard measurement uncertainty below 10 percent of the concentration, with a relaxed limit of 50 percent for very low amount fractions (10 nmol/mol or below). Laboratories must prepare a validation report documenting these evaluations.
It further lists suitable analytical techniques—such as gas chromatography (with various detectors), FTIR spectroscopy, cavity ring-down spectroscopy, and electrochemical sensors—for measuring specific impurities (water, hydrocarbons, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, sulphur compounds, formaldehyde, ammonia, and halogenated compounds) against their respective ISO 14687 grade D thresholds. Guidance is also provided on sampling strategy, sampling vessels, sample handling, and the content required in analytical reports.

title: Standard of the Month - Bureau of Indian Standards
content:
Standard of the Month
IS 17017 (Part 23) : 2026
Electric Vehicle Conductive Charging System
Part 23 d.c. Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment(IEC 61851-23 : 2023, MOD) ( First Revision )
This Indian Standard is a modified adoption of IEC 61851-23:2023 and specifies requirements for DC Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) — the equipment that transfers energy between the supply network and electric vehicles for DC charging. It applies to equipment with a rated maximum voltage of up to 1000 V AC or 1500 V DC on the grid side and up to 1500 V DC on the vehicle side, covering Systems A and C as defined in the IEC document; System B has been excluded as unsuitable for Indian conditions. Ambient test temperature has been raised to 55°C from the IEC’s 40°C, and system voltages are aligned with IS 12360.
This revision adds several new safety requirements over the earlier edition, including equipotential bonding and protective-conductor impedance checks on the vehicle side, strain relief and surface-temperature limits for vehicle-side cable assemblies, emergency shutdown provisions for short-circuit faults, under-voltage protection at the vehicle connector, and requirements for temperature-controlled energy transfer.
This covers classification of EVSE, charging modes and functions, digital communication with the vehicle, protection against electric shock (basic, fault and enhanced protection), cable assembly and constructional requirements, overload and short-circuit protection, automatic reclosing, emergency disconnection, and marking and instructions. Detailed normative annexes specify circuit diagrams, control sequences and safety measures for Systems A, B and C, along with test methods, technical data and bidirectional power transfer provisions. It is to be read together with IS 17017 (Part 1):2018.

title: What is Hallmarking?
content:
Q: What is Hallmarking?
A: Hallmarking is the accurate determination and official recording of the proportionate content of precious metal in precious metal articles (as per IS 15820). Hallmarks are thus official marks used in India as a guarantee of purity or fineness of precious metal articles.

title: Which precious metals are hallmarked in India?
content:
Q: Which precious metals are hallmarked in India?
A: In India, at present two precious metals namely gold and silver have been brought under the purview of Hallmarking.

title: What are the Indian Standards on Hallmarking?
content:
Q: What are the Indian Standards on Hallmarking?
A: IS 1417: 2016 Gold and Gold Alloys, Jewellery/Artefacts-Fineness and Marking- Specification IS 2112:2014 Silver and Silver Alloys, Jewellery/Artefacts-Fineness and Marking- Specification IS 15820: 2009 General Requirements for establishment and operation of Assaying and operation of Assaying and Hallmarking centres. IS 1418: 2009 Determination of gold in gold bullion, gold alloys and gold jewellery/artefacts-cupellation( Fire Assay) Method IS 2113: 2014 Assaying Silver in Silver and Silver Alloys-Methods. IS 17278:2019 Refined Gold and Silver Bars for Good Delivery — Specification

title: What are the grades permitted for hallmarking of Gold/Silver jewellery/Artefacts?
content:
Q: What are the grades permitted for hallmarking of Gold/Silver jewellery/Artefacts?
A: IS 1417:2016 permits hallmarking of six caratage (fineness in ppt) of gold jewellery/artefacts, viz. 14K(585), 18K(750), 20K(833), 22K(916), 23K(958) and 24KS(995). IS 2112 : 2014 permits hallmarking of of six grades(fineness in ppt) of silver jewellery/artefacts, viz. 800(800.0), 835(835.0), 900(900.0), 925(925.0), 970(970.0) and 990(990.0)

title: What are the objectives behind instituting Hallmarking Scheme?
content:
Q: What are the objectives behind instituting Hallmarking Scheme?
A: Objectives of Hallmarking scheme are to protect consumer against malpractices in gold/silver related to purity, to develop India as a leading gold market centre in the World and to develop export competitiveness.

title: What are the benefits to Customer from purchasing hallmarked jewellery?
content:
Q: What are the benefits to Customer from purchasing hallmarked jewellery?
A: Hallmarked jewellery provides third party assurance and satisfaction that customer gets right purity of gold/silver for the given price (value for money).

title: How will the jewellers benefit from getting registration/certification from BIS ?
content:
Q: How will the jewellers benefit from getting registration/certification from BIS ?
A: It will provide clear indication of his capability, strong evidence of commitment to quality and assurance of consistency in purity and quality of gold/silver jewellery.

title: What is HUID in the hallmarked gold jewellery?
content:
Q: What is HUID in the hallmarked gold jewellery?
A: HUID is a Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) number and it is one of the components of hallmark. It is a six-digit alphanumeric number which is unique for each hallmarked item and is traceable. Customer can also verify the HUID number in the BIS Care App using the ‘Verify HUID’ feature.

title: What does hallmark on gold jewellery consist of?
content:
Q: What does hallmark on gold jewellery consist of?
A: Since the introduction of HUID (i.e. 1st July 2021) hallmark consists of 3 marks viz, BIS logo, purity of the article in caratage as well as fineness and six-digit alphanumeric HUID number.

title: Who operates the Hallmarking Scheme?
content:
Q: Who operates the Hallmarking Scheme?
A: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Standing Committee on Gold and Precious Metals, identified Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) in the year 2000 as the sole agency to operate the Hallmarking Scheme in India, and entrusted BIS with the task of implementing hallmarking scheme to protect the consumer against malpractices and develop export competitiveness and make India a leading market for gold jewellery in the world. BIS through its network of Regional/ Branch offices all over the country operates the Hallmarking Scheme for gold and silver jewellery.

title: How much does it cost to get a gold/silver article hallmarked?
content:
Q: How much does it cost to get a gold/silver article hallmarked?
A: i) Following hallmarking charges are applicable for gold articles: » Rs. 45/- per article » Minimum charges for a consignment shall be Rs. 200/- (Services Tax and other levies as applicable shall be extra) ii) Following hallmarking charges are applicable for silver articles: » Rs. 35/- per article » Minimum charges for a consignment shall be Rs. 150.00. (Services Tax and other levies as applicable shall be extra) Note- • Consignment – A consignment shall be collection of articles/artifacts of same fineness from which a sample shall be drawn and assayed to determine conformance with the acceptable criteria. There may be different lots in a consignment. • Lot – A lot shall be defined as set of articles having same fineness, type/design

title: Does Hallmark charges include making charges and wastage charges?
content:
Q: Does Hallmark charges include making charges and wastage charges?
A: No. No.

title: Are the hallmarking charges dependent on weight of jewellery?
content:
Q: Are the hallmarking charges dependent on weight of jewellery?
A: No, hallmarking charges are paid per article irrespective of the weight of the article.

title: Is it necessary to take authentic bills/invoice for the hallmarked article from retailer/jeweller?
content:
Q: Is it necessary to take authentic bills/invoice for the hallmarked article from retailer/jeweller?
A: Yes, it is necessary to take authentic bills/invoice of the hallmarked article from retailer/jeweller.

title: Is it necessary to have details of hallmarked articles in the bill/invoice issued by jeweller/retailer?
content:
Q: Is it necessary to have details of hallmarked articles in the bill/invoice issued by jeweller/retailer?
A: Yes, it is necessary to have details of hallmarked articles in the bill/invoice issued by jeweller/retailer for any dispute/misuse/complaint redressal.

title: What should be looked at in a jewellery shop while purchasing the hallmarked jewellery?
content:
Q: What should be looked at in a jewellery shop while purchasing the hallmarked jewellery?
A: On the outside of the sales outlet, the registered/certified jeweller shall display the logo of BIS with the wording “Hallmarked jewellery available for sale”. Certificate of registration issued by BIS shall be displayed by the jeweller in a jewellery shop. Jeweller shall have magnifying glass of minimum 10X magnification to show hallmark to customer in the hallmarked jewellery. Relation of fineness with caratage shall be displayed by the jeweller.

title: What control BIS has on registered/certified Jewellers and Recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres?
content:
Q: What control BIS has on registered/certified Jewellers and Recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres?
A: BIS carries out regular surveillance audit of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres as well as draws market samples from registered/certified jewellers for testing in BIS referral assay labs (RALs).

title: What are the permissible sizes(height) of hallmark on gold/silver articles?
content:
Q: What are the permissible sizes(height) of hallmark on gold/silver articles?
A: The permissible sizes (height) of the hallmark are : For Gold(mm) For Silver(mm) 1.5 4.0 1.0 2.0 0.75 1.5 0.5 1.0 – 0.75 The permissible sizes (height) of the hallmark are :

title: Is it necessary to have hallmark on both the articles/jewellery in pairs and on all detachable parts?
content:
Q: Is it necessary to have hallmark on both the articles/jewellery in pairs and on all detachable parts?
A: Yes, each article in pair and all detachable parts should have hallmark with different HUIDs. Customer should look for hallmarking and fineness details in each article to prevent any misuse w.r.t fineness/purity.

title: What is the detachable part in jewellery?
content:
Q: What is the detachable part in jewellery?
A: Detachable part in jewellery is any part which can be easily removed or replaced.

title: Can an artisan or common man directly approach the A&H centre for hallmarking of the jewellery?
content:
Q: Can an artisan or common man directly approach the A&H centre for hallmarking of the jewellery?
A: No, only BIS registered/certified jewellers can approach the A&H centre for hallmarking of the jewellery.

title: Where can a common person get information on hallmarking?
content:
Q: Where can a common person get information on hallmarking?
A: All the information regarding hallmarking in detail has been provided at BIS website: www.bis.gov.in under hallmarking section. The information includes general information on hallmarking, hallmarking regulation, mandatory hallmarking orders, procedure and guidelines for Jewellers and hallmarking centres, all the forms and list of registered jewellers as well as hallmarking centres etc.

title: Where can one get the list of BIS Registered jewellers?
content:
Q: Where can one get the list of BIS Registered jewellers?
A: The list of BIS Registered/certified jewellers is available on BIS website under hallmarking section and can be directly accessed by following the link https://www.bis.gov.in/index.php/hallmarking-overview/jewellers-registration-scheme/list-of-licensed-jewellers//

title: Where can one get the list of BIS Recognized Assaying and Hallmarking centres?
content:
Q: Where can one get the list of BIS Recognized Assaying and Hallmarking centres?
A: The list of BIS Recognized Assaying and Hallmarking centres is available on BIS website under hallmarking section and can be directly accessed by following the link: https://www.manakonline.in/MANAK/AHCListForWebsite

title: Is it possible for the common man to get his/her hallmarked jewellery tested for purity from an A&H centre?
content:
Q: Is it possible for the common man to get his/her hallmarked jewellery tested for purity from an A&H centre?
A: Yes, after paying testing charges of Rs. 200(for testing by fire assay method as per IS 1418) to any of BIS recognized A&H centre. The list of BIS recognized A&H centre is available at BIS website www.bis.gov.in under the hallmarking section.

title: Hallmarking overview - Bureau of Indian Standards
content: Hallmarking is the accurate determination and official recording of the proportionate content of precious metal in precious metal articles. Hallmarks are thus official marks used in many countries as a guarantee of purity or fineness of precious metal articles. The principle objectives of the Hallmarking Scheme are to protect the public against adulteration and to obligate manufacturers to maintain legal standards of fineness. In India, at present two precious metals namely gold and silver have been brought under the purview of Hallmarking.

title: Cement (Quality Control) Order, 2003
content: This Quality Control Order, issued under the erstwhile BIS Act, makes BIS certification mandatory for all varieties of cement manufactured or sold in India, including Ordinary Portland Cement, Portland Pozzolana Cement, Portland Slag Cement, Sulphate Resisting Portland Cement, White Portland Cement, Oil Well Cement and several other cement grades. Manufacturers and importers must hold a valid BIS licence and bear the ISI mark before sale. Gazette Notification: S.O. 191(E), dated 17 February 2003. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards / Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Status: in force.

title: Electrical Wires, Cables, Appliances and Protection Devices and Accessories (Quality Control) Order, 2003
content: This order mandates BIS certification for a wide range of household electrical goods sold in India, covering residual current circuit breakers, AC watt-hour meters, self-ballasted lamps, electric irons, immersion water heaters, room heaters, domestic switches, tungsten filament lamps, PVC-insulated cables and related overcurrent protection devices. It has been amended several times since 2003 to update the list of covered Indian Standards. Gazette Notification: S.O. 189(E), dated 17 February 2003, with subsequent amendments in 2004, 2005, 2009 and 2010. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards / Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Status: in force, amended.

title: Multi-Purpose Dry Batteries (Quality Control) Order
content: This order requires multi-purpose dry batteries sold in India to conform to Indian Standard IS 8144 and to carry the BIS Standard Mark under a valid licence, making it one of the earliest product-specific Quality Control Orders issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards. Gazette Notification: S.O. 516(E), dated 25 May 1987. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards / Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Status: in force.

title: The Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992
content: This Act of Parliament regulates the production, supply and distribution of infant milk substitutes, feeding bottles and infant foods in India. It underpins the compulsory BIS certification requirement for plastic and glass feeding bottles (covering Indian Standards IS 14625 and IS 5168), restricting their manufacture and sale to products that meet the relevant Indian Standards. Gazette Notification: Act No. 41 of 1992. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Women and Child Development, Government of India. Status: in force.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Women and Child Development, Government of India)

title: Oil Pressure Stoves (Quality Control) Order, 1997
content: This order makes BIS certification compulsory for oil pressure stoves sold in India, including offset-burner type stoves, multi-burner stoves and standard oil pressure stoves, requiring manufacturers to hold a BIS licence and mark products with the Standard Mark. Gazette Notification: S.O. 451(E), dated 16 June 1997. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards / Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Status: in force.

title: Pneumatic Tyres and Tubes for Automotive Vehicles (Quality Control) Order, 2009
content: This order requires pneumatic tyres and tubes used on automotive vehicles, including two- and three-wheelers, passenger cars and commercial vehicles, to comply with the relevant Indian Standards and carry the BIS Standard Mark before sale in India. It has been amended twice since its original notification. Gazette Notification: S.O. 2953(E), dated 19 November 2009, amended by S.O. 1057(E) dated 11 May 2010 and S.O. 2758(E) dated 9 November 2010. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards / Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Status: in force, amended.

title: Gas Cylinder Rules, 2016 (under the Explosives Act, 1884)
content: These rules, framed under the Explosives Act, 1884, mandate BIS certification for LPG containers, cylinder valves, regulators and related fittings used for automotive and domestic purposes, covering a large family of Indian Standards for welded and seamless steel gas cylinders. The rules have been amended twice in 2026 to update technical and safety requirements. Gazette Notification: G.S.R. No. 1081(E), dated 22 November 2016, amended by G.S.R. 315(E) dated 28 April 2026 and G.S.R. 447(E) dated 5 June 2026. Issuing Authority: Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Status: in force, amended.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), Ministry of Commerce and Industry)

title: Clinical Thermometers (Quality Control) Order, 2001
content: This order makes it mandatory for solid-stem and enclosed-scale clinical thermometers sold in India to conform to the relevant Indian Standards and bear the BIS Standard Mark under a valid licence. Gazette Notification: GSR No. 843(E), dated 9 November 2001. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards / Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Status: in force.

title: Quality Control Requirement for Diagnostic Medical X-Ray Equipment
content: This requirement, issued by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, mandates conformity of diagnostic medical X-ray equipment to Indian Standard IS 7620 (Part 1), forming part of the compulsory certification regime for medical equipment sold and used in India. Gazette Notification: AERB/443/39/MDX/3509/94, dated October 1994. Issuing Authority: Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). Status: in force.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB))

title: Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Order, 2024
content: This order, the current consolidated version of a series of steel QCOs issued since 2020, makes BIS certification mandatory for a large range of steel and iron products sold in India, including structural steel, reinforcement bars, wire rods, pressure-vessel plates, galvanized sheets and electrical steel. It replaces earlier 2020 orders and has itself been amended in 2025 and 2026. Gazette Notification: S.O. 3716(E), dated 29 August 2024. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Steel, Government of India. Status: in force, amended. Supersedes: Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Order, 2020 (S.O. 756(E) and successive orders dated 2020).
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Steel, Government of India)

title: Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Amendment Order, 2025
content: This notification amends the Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Order, 2024, updating the list of Indian Standards and implementation timelines covered under the mandatory steel certification regime. Gazette Notification: S.O. 5134(E), dated 20 November 2025. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Steel, Government of India. Status: in force. Amends: Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Order, 2024 (S.O. 3716(E)).
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Steel, Government of India)

title: Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Amendment Order, 2026
content: This notification further amends the Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Order, 2024, revising the scope or implementation dates for specific steel product standards under the mandatory certification regime. Gazette Notification: S.O. 3300(E), dated 22 June 2026. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Steel, Government of India. Status: in force. Amends: Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Order, 2024 (S.O. 3716(E)).
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Steel, Government of India)

title: Toys (Quality Control) Order, 2020
content: This order makes BIS certification mandatory for toys intended for use by children under 14 years of age, requiring conformity to Indian Standards covering physical, chemical and electrical safety of toys and use of the ISI mark under a BIS licence. It came into force on 1 January 2021 and has since been amended several times, including in 2024. Gazette Notification: S.O. 853(E), dated 25 February 2020, amended by S.O. 3146(E) dated 15 September 2020, S.O. 4514(E) dated 11 December 2020, and S.O. 4277(E) dated 30 September 2024. Issuing Authority: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Status: in force, amended.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry)

title: Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement of Compulsory Registration) Order, 2021
content: This is the current governing order for the BIS Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS) covering electronics and IT goods, including mobile phones, laptops, televisions, power adapters, power banks, LED lighting products, UPS systems and other consumer electronics. Manufacturers must register products with BIS and self-declare conformity to the applicable Indian Standards. It supersedes the original 2012 CRS order and has been amended multiple times to add new product categories. Gazette Notification: Notification dated November 2021, amended by S.O. 1246(E) dated 10 March 2026 and other product-specific amendments. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Status: in force, amended. Supersedes: Electronics & Information Technology Goods (Requirements for Compulsory Registration) Order, 2012 (S.O. 2357(E)).
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY))

title: Amendments to the Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirements for Compulsory Registration) Order, 2021
content: This notification amends the 2021 Electronics and IT Goods Compulsory Registration Order, updating the schedule of covered product categories and applicable Indian Standards under the CRS scheme administered by MeitY. Gazette Notification: S.O. 1246(E), dated 10 March 2026. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Status: in force. Amends: Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement of Compulsory Registration) Order, 2021.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY))

title: Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirements for Compulsory Registration) Order, 2012
content: This was the original order establishing the Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS) for electronics and IT goods in India, first notified in 2012 and requiring self-declaration of conformity for products such as video games, LCD/LED televisions and optical disc players. It has since been superseded by the 2021 CRS order. Gazette Notification: S.O. 2357(E), dated 7 September 2012. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Status: superseded. Superseded by: Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement of Compulsory Registration) Order, 2021.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY))

title: Mobile Phone Handsets (Indian Language Support) Notification
content: This notification, issued under the CRS framework, required mobile phone handsets sold in India to support Indian languages as specified in IS 16333 (Part 3), with an implementation date of 1 July 2017. The requirement has since been folded into the 2021 Electronics and IT Goods CRS Order. Gazette Notification: Notification dated 24 October 2016. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Status: superseded. Superseded by: Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement of Compulsory Registration) Order, 2021.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY))

title: Digital Television Receiver for Satellite Broadcast Transmission – CRS Amendment Order, 2023
content: This amendment to the 2021 Electronics and IT Goods CRS Order brought television sets under mandatory registration against Indian Standard IS 18112:2022 for digital television receivers for satellite broadcast transmission, with implementation timelines subsequently extended through 2025 and 2026 notifications. Gazette Notification: S.O. 1929(E), dated 26 April 2023, with implementation extensions in 2025 and 2026. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Status: in force, amended.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY))

title: Solar Photovoltaics, Systems, Devices and Components Goods (Requirements for Compulsory Registration) Order, 2017
content: This order establishes the Compulsory Registration Scheme for solar photovoltaic modules, inverters and related components sold in India, covering crystalline silicon and thin-film PV modules, power converters and islanding-prevention test procedures for grid-connected inverters. It has been amended several times, most recently in 2025 to cover larger-capacity solar inverters. Gazette Notification: S.O. 2920(E), dated 30 August 2017, with amendments through 2025. Issuing Authority: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). Status: in force, amended.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE))

title: Solar Systems, Devices and Components Goods Order, 2025
content: This order extends the Compulsory Registration Scheme for solar products to solar photovoltaic inverters with capacity greater than 200 kW, requiring registration with BIS before such inverters can be manufactured or sold in India. Gazette Notification: S.O. 3597(E), dated 5 August 2025. Issuing Authority: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). Status: in force.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE))

title: Ortho Phosphoric Acid (Quality Control) Order, 2021
content: This order makes BIS certification mandatory for Ortho Phosphoric Acid conforming to Indian Standard IS 798:2020, as part of the government's programme to bring major chemicals under compulsory quality control. It has been amended multiple times between 2021 and 2024. Gazette Notification: S.O. 2335(E), dated 15 June 2021, amended by S.O. 4914(E) 2021, and further amendments in 2022 and 2024. Issuing Authority: Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. Status: in force, amended.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers)

title: Polyphosphoric Acid (Quality Control) Order, 2021
content: This order mandates BIS certification for Polyphosphoric Acid conforming to Indian Standard IS 17439:2020, requiring domestic and overseas manufacturers to obtain a BIS licence before selling the chemical in India. Gazette Notification: S.O. 5388(E), dated 24 December 2021, amended in May 2022. Issuing Authority: Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. Status: in force, amended.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers)

title: Trimethyl Phosphite (Quality Control) Order, 2022
content: This order requires Trimethyl Phosphite, Technical Grade, sold or manufactured in India to conform to Indian Standard IS 17412:2020 and to be certified by BIS, as part of the government's chemicals quality-control programme. Gazette Notification: S.O. 1637(E), dated 5 April 2022. Issuing Authority: Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. Status: in force.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers)

title: Cotton Bales (Quality Control) Order, 2023
content: This order makes BIS certification mandatory for cotton bales conforming to Indian Standard IS 12171:2019, part of the Ministry of Textiles' effort to standardise raw cotton quality in India. It has been amended repeatedly since 2023, including a notification in 2026 rescinding part of the order. Gazette Notification: S.O. 948(E), dated 28 February 2023, with multiple amendments through 2026. Issuing Authority: Ministry of Textiles, Government of India. Status: amended / partly rescinded.
source_name: Bureau of Indian Standards (Ministry of Textiles, Government of India)

title: Guidance Document on Quality Control Orders (QCOs)
content: This BIS-published guidance document explains the legal basis of Quality Control Orders under the BIS Act, 2016, how QCOs are proposed and notified by line ministries, the licensing and enforcement process, and how manufacturers and importers can determine whether a product is covered by a QCO. Gazette Notification: Published by BIS, revised version. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). Status: in force.

title: Products under Compulsory Certification - Scheme Overview
content: This BIS overview page explains that while BIS certification is generally voluntary, the Central Government can make conformity to Indian Standards compulsory for specific products in the interest of public safety, health, environment, fair trade or national security. It sets out the four mandatory certification schemes operated by BIS: Scheme-I (ISI Mark Scheme), Scheme-II (Registration Scheme / CRS), Scheme-IV (Certificate of Conformity) and Scheme-X (Certification), and links to the current list of QCO-covered products under each. Gazette Notification: N/A. Issuing Authority: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). Status: in force.

title: Helmet for Riders of Two-Wheeler Motor Vehicles (Quality Control) Order, 2020
content: This Quality Control Order makes BIS certification mandatory for protective helmets used by riders of two-wheeler motor vehicles in India. Helmets must conform to IS 4151:2015 'Protective Helmet for Two Wheeler Riders - Specification (Fourth Revision)', which sets requirements for materials, construction, workmanship, finish and performance (impact absorption, penetration resistance, retention system strength, peripheral vision, and a maximum mass of 1500 g), and must bear the ISI mark under a licence from BIS. The Order was issued by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) and took effect from 1 March 2021. Only BIS-certified/ISI-marked helmets may be manufactured, sold or imported in India; the requirement is separately reinforced by Motor Vehicles Act helmet-wearing rules.
gazette_note: Order and IS 4151:2015 linkage and 1 March 2021 effective date are corroborated by multiple independent sources; the specific MoRTH gazette S.O./G.S.R. number was not confirmed and should be verified against the official e-Gazette before relying on it for legal citation.

title: Domestic Pressure Cooker (Quality Control) Order, 2020
content: This Quality Control Order, issued by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, under Section 14 of the erstwhile BIS Act after consulting BIS, makes BIS certification mandatory for domestic pressure cookers. Cookers must comply with IS 2347:2017 'Domestic Pressure Cooker - Specification' (subsequently revised as IS 2347:2023), which covers body/lid/gasket materials (aluminium alloy or stainless steel), nominal capacity range (1-22 litres), the fusible safety-plug/pressure-release mechanism, and bursting-pressure and lid-removal safety tests, and must bear the ISI mark under a Scheme-I licence from BIS. The Order was notified on 21 January 2020. Its stated purpose is to remove substandard and potentially unsafe (explosion-risk) pressure cookers from the Indian market.
gazette_note: DPIIT issuance, 21 Jan 2020 notification date and IS 2347 linkage are corroborated by multiple sources; the specific S.O. gazette number was not confirmed and should be verified against the official e-Gazette.

title: Footwear made from Leather and other Materials (Quality Control) Order, 2024
content: Issued by DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, this Order mandates BIS certification for approximately 11-12 categories of leather and other-material footwear (e.g. leather safety/dress/casual footwear), which must conform to the relevant product-specific Indian Standards (drawing on the IS 15298 footwear-testing series among others) and bear the ISI mark. The Order came into force on 1 August 2024. A subsequent amendment permitted non-compliant stock manufactured/imported before that date to be sold until 31 July 2026. Micro and small manufacturing units are exempted from this QCO.
gazette_note: Order title, 1 Aug 2024 effective date and MSME exemption corroborated by multiple independent sources (incl. Council for Leather Exports); exact S.O. gazette number not confirmed here.

title: Footwear made from All Rubber and all Polymeric Material and its Components (Quality Control) Order, 2024
content: Issued by DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, this Order mandates BIS certification for footwear made wholly of rubber or polymeric material (e.g. gumboots, PVC/hawai chappals, rubber slippers, industrial rubber boots) and covers roughly 13 footwear products plus 4 outsole component items, which must conform to applicable Indian Standards (including IS 10702 for rubber chappals and IS 11544 for PU slippers) and bear the ISI mark. Originally issued 15 March 2024 and effective 1 August 2024, it was amended by S.O. 3701(E) dated 30 August 2024, which extended the permitted sell-through period for existing non-compliant stock to 31 July 2026. The 4 outsole items are permitted for import only for use in export-bound footwear production, not for domestic sale.
gazette_note: Amendment gazette number S.O. 3701(E) dated 30 August 2024 corroborated by an independent source; the ORIGINAL March 2024 notification's own S.O. number was not separately confirmed.

title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Footwear (Quality Control) Order, 2020
content: Issued by DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Order No. 33004/99, dated 27 October 2020), this Order mandates BIS certification for safety footwear, protective footwear and occupational footwear (personal protective equipment for industrial/workplace use), which must conform to the relevant IS 15298 series requirements and bear the ISI mark under a BIS licence before manufacture, import or sale in India.
gazette_note: Order No. 33004/99 dated 27 October 2020, as listed by the Council for Leather Exports (an industry export-promotion body under the Ministry of Commerce).

title: Cookware, Utensils and Cans for Food and Beverages (Quality Control) Order, 2026
content: Issued by the Ministry of Steel under Sections 16, 17 and 25(3) of the BIS Act, 2016, this Order replaces the earlier stainless-steel-utensils QCO and mandates BIS certification for steel cookware, kitchen utensils, and cans used for packaging food and beverages, requiring conformity to the applicable Indian Standards for stainless-steel utensils and bearing of the ISI mark. Products that are themselves filled with solid, liquid or gas contents at the point of sale are excluded from the Order's scope. It came into effect on 1 October 2025, with transitional relief for stock manufactured or imported before that date.
gazette_note: Only a single secondary source was found for this entry; issuing ministry, scope and 1 Oct 2025 effective date should be cross-checked against the official Ministry of Steel/BIS gazette notification before relying on it.

title: Transition Facilitation (Quality Control) Order, 2026
content: Issued by DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and published in the Official Gazette as S.O. 3417(E) dated 25 June 2026, this Order does not itself impose new product standards; it introduces a risk-based alternative compliance mechanism allowing eligible domestic industry to source supplies from BIS-licensed manufacturers under Scheme-II (instead of Scheme-I/ISI Mark) while their own certification is being processed, easing a common bottleneck for existing QCOs. It applies to companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 that can demonstrate technical capability and a compliance record, and covers 10 QCOs already in force, spanning toys, footwear, air conditioners, furniture, hinges, water heaters, washing machines and household electrical appliances. This confirms that separate QCOs for furniture, air conditioners, hinges, washing machines and water heaters exist and are in force, but this knowledge base does not yet contain individually verified records for each of those underlying QCOs -- see coverage_note.
coverage_note: This record confirms the EXISTENCE of in-force QCOs for furniture, air conditioners, hinges, washing machines and household water heaters, but this knowledge base does not yet contain a dedicated, individually-verified record for each of those underlying orders (their own gazette numbers, effective dates and covered IS standards). Treat 'furniture/AC/hinges/washing machine/water heater is QCO-covered' as confirmed, but verify the specific order text against the DPIIT/BIS gazette database before citing it in a compliance determination.
gazette_note: Gazette citation S.O. 3417(E) dated 25 June 2026 corroborated by two independent sources.
